en: In the preface to *Coarse Words on the Buddha-Dharma and Subtle Utterances*, Master Lianxi states that all words, whether coarse or subtle, ultimately converge upon the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). All his poems and verses clearly elucidate the fundamental school;
they flow forth from a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), establish their teachings based upon the sūtras, and extol the samādhi of buddha-remembrance (*nienfo sanmei*).
These are the remaining aggregates. Herein, for the guidance of beginners, we borrow words to clarify the mind and rely on speech to perceive the Way.
Once the Way is perceived, words vanish; this is what is meant by "being identical with words, yet not being words.

(Guangru) Having frequently observed that beginners have not yet been able to read the various scriptures of the Pure Land school and find it difficult to memorize them, I have therefore selected from among the hymns of the Pure Land tradition those which I have already personally examined.
I have recorded these teachings as I encountered them and carved them into woodblocks for circulation, so that they may be easily read and recited.
Should there be those who prefer concise practice, even a single word or half a verse is sufficient to rely upon for the purpose of resolving the cycle of birth and death. In our own dynasty...
Emperor Shizong Xian, in his preface to the poems of the Great Being Hanshan, stated:
"Readers may regard them as vernacular speech, or as rhymed verse, or as doctrinal discourse, or as Chan language. Like a mani jewel, its substance is not of a single color;
it is perfectly round in every respect, appearing according to what the eyes of each person behold. I, the Emperor, consider them to be neither vernacular nor rhymed, neither..."

This teaching is not mere meditation; it is indeed the direct mind and direct speech of the ancient Buddhas. The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean, and this selection from it is but a single drop within that sea.
I am personally ashamed that my Dharma-eye is not yet clear, and thus I cannot help but feel the regret of having missed some pearls.
One must certainly not regard this as the ultimate truth, nor should one disregard this book because its author is of humble station. I have once seen...
The Verse Praise for Master Ouyi’s Western Chamber, which states in brief: "By means of these subtle and wondrous gāthās, may I read and recite them as I study.
Reading once, reading twice, the dust-like thoughts vanish; Reading three times, reading four times, defiled passions grow thin.

When one reaches ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a million recitations, This very body shall already have been entrusted to a lotus flower. I also vow that those who read and recite hereafter [shall likewise attain this]."
Together we shall ultimately be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This serves as the preface.
Written by Guanru on the Buddha’s Day of Joy in the seventh month of the Bingxu year of the Guangxu era at the Yangzhou Tripitaka Library.
Liuxiu must read this.
From the *Quan Tang Shi*, Master Hanshan:
Human life does not exceed a hundred years, yet one constantly harbors anxieties for a thousand autumns. When one’s own body first falls ill, one then begins to worry for one’s descendants.
Looking down at the roots of the grain in the soil, looking up at the tops of the mulberry trees; the scale-weight falls into the Eastern Sea, and only upon reaching the bottom does one know rest.
The evil realms are vast and boundless, dark and shadowy with no sunlight; eight hundred years in the human world do not equal even half a night there.
These ignorant children are most pitiable when one considers their plight. I urge you to seek liberation and recognize the King of Dharma.
The suffering of saṃsāra is terrifying; its cycles of coming and going are like tossing dust, never ceasing as it swirls around like ants on a trail. The six realms are in utter chaos.
Though you change your head and alter your face, you are not someone other than the person of old. Swiftly resolve the dark prison; do not allow your mind-nature to grow dull.
There is a certain kind of person in the world who drifts along like a block of wood; when they speak, they have no understanding, saying, "I am not worried about anything."
When asked about the Way, the Way is not found; when asked about the Buddha, the Buddha is not sought. If one searches for them with meticulous scrutiny, there is only a state of bewildered sorrow.
I find joy in the Way of my entire life, amidst misty vines and stone caves. My wild nature is largely unrestrained and expansive, forever accompanied by the leisure of white clouds.
There is a path that does not lead to the world; with no mind, who can reach it? Sitting alone upon a stone bed through the night, the full moon rises over Cold Mountain.
The waters of the great ocean are boundless, filled with tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of fish and dragons, devouring one another—a chaotic mass of deluded flesh.
Because the mind does not understand or sever [delusion], false thoughts arise like smoke. The moon of nature is limpid and bright; it shines vast and boundlessly.
Like so many precious treasures on a ruined ship in the ocean—the mast lost in front and the rudder missing behind—[one drifts aimlessly].
Tumbling and turning, left to the whims of the wind; rising and falling, tossed by the waves. How can one reach the shore? Strive on; do not sit idly still!
Human life amidst the dust and obscurity is just like a worm in a basin: all day long it wanders about, never leaving that basin.
The immortal cannot be attained; afflictions are reckoned to be endless. The years and months flow like a stream; in an instant, one becomes an old man.
When Hanshan utters these words, he again resembles a madman. To speak of matters face-to-face is why he incurs the resentment of many.
The mind is truly what produces speech; a straightforward mind has no front or back. When facing death, what can be done? Who is the cowardly wretch?
On the dark path to the underworld, one is bound by the constraints of karma.

Those of superior capacity possess minds that are fierce and sharp; upon hearing it once, they immediately know its subtlety. Those of middling capacity possess pure minds; through careful reflection, they realize it is most essential.
Those of inferior capacity are dull, dark, and deluded; their stubborn skin is most difficult to pierce. Only when blood flows profusely do they finally realize they must destroy themselves.
Look at this thief with open eyes; in the bustling marketplace, he makes his decisions. Corpses are discarded like dust—whom can one speak to at such a time?
A manly great hero cuts through [the world] in two pieces with a single stroke. With a human face but the heart of a beast, when will the creation of evil ever cease?

How lamentable are those who drift in this transient life! How many days will pass before it ends? Morning after morning there is no moment of leisure; year after year one does not realize they are growing old.

It is all for the sake of seeking food and clothing, which gives rise to human afflictions. For a thousand or ten thousand years of restless turmoil, one wanders between coming and going through the three evil realms.

I urge you to cease and desist; do not trouble the Old Lord Yama. If you lose your footing, you will enter the three paths of suffering; your bones will be ground to powder as you undergo a thousand beatings.
You will become an inhabitant of hell forever, eternally severed from the path of this present life. To spare you from believing my words, recognize the treasure within your own robes.
In this world there are many who understand; yet the ignorant toil in vain suffering. They do not seek goodness for the future, but know only how to create the causes of evil.
Those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten non-virtues take the three poisons as their kin; once dead, they enter hell, remaining there as long as silver stored in a treasury.
Anger is the fire within the mind; it can burn down the forest of merit. Those who wish to practice the Bodhisattva path must protect their true heart through patience.

With over one hundred years of life spent in old age and illness, my face is yellowed and my hair is white; I prefer the seclusion of the mountains. Clad in coarse cloth robes, I pass my days according to conditions;
how could I envy the clever fashions of the world? People exhaust their minds and spirits for the sake of fame and profit, advancing with a hundred kinds of greed.
One’s own body is a fleeting illusion, like the remains of a lamp's wick. To have one's body buried within a tomb—what is there to be called existence or non-existence?
What is there for worldly people to lament? Suffering and pleasure sear one another without end. Through how many kalpas have we wandered through birth and death?
East, west, south, and north—whose home is it? Zhang, Wang, Li, and Zhao are merely temporary surnames; as for the affairs of the six realms and the three paths...
It is like sesame seeds; it is simply because the master does not realize the ultimate cessation that he invites transmigration and decline, chasing after delusion and heterodoxy.
On the peak of Cold Mountain, the lunar disc stands solitary; it illuminates the empty sky where not a single thing exists.
This precious, natural, priceless treasure is buried within the five aggregates, drowning the physical body.

Furthermore, the Great Being Shide lamented upon seeing the people of the world: "Every single one loves to eat meat; their bowls and plates never dry. For a long time they say they are not satisfied.

Yesterday they prepared a vegetarian feast, yet this morning they slaughter six domestic animals. This is entirely because they are dragged along by the force of karma; it is not a matter of their own desires."
Once you have built a heavenly palace, a hundred times you shall build a hell. When the messengers of Yama come to pursue you, the whole family will weep together.
You shall be made to warm yourself by the furnace and bathe within the cauldron; even when you emerge from it, your clothes shall be changed for others.
Shutting one's door to commit sins in secret, hoping thereby to evade calamity; yet the wicked minions of Yama seize the records and report them to King Yama.

Even if one does not enter the boiling cauldron, one must still lie upon the iron bed. It is not permitted to hire another to take one’s place; for what one has done oneself, one must undergo oneself.
The three realms are like a turning wheel; fleeting life is like flowing water. All the various species of sentient beings, craving life, do not perceive death.
Behold the dew hanging at dawn: how long can its drops endure?
The path of the ancient Buddhas is desolate; the ignorant person arrives only to be lost. It is solely because of the weight of past karma that they are unable to know.
If you wish to recognize the principle of non-action, let not a single thread hang in your mind. Study with diligent effort throughout every life, and you will surely behold our Teacher.
In the style of Hanshan’s poems, Chan Master Chushi wrote:

Since beginningless time, I have fallen into a vast, desolate void. By what means can the light of wisdom be brought forth? In the human realm, one grieves that the days are short; Beneath the earth, one laments that time is long.
Myriad waters flow toward the eastern ocean; all the stars revolve around the North Pole. Throughout the vast expanse of heaven and earth, by whose power is this ultimately sustained?

Those who study the Way today are exhausted before they have even reached their limit. That those who practice through immeasurable kalpas have succeeded is entirely due to the power of their valor and diligence.
The tongue is the root of rise and fall; the mind is the source of fortune and calamity. All things are created by oneself; who says they belong to Heaven and Earth?
Planting blessings is like planting trees; planting virtue is like planting grain. Once what has been accumulated is sufficient, there will be no lack of what is needed.
One should seek to attain Buddhahood early; thus one will naturally possess supramundane merit. If one possesses worldly merit alone, it is in vain that the three poisons grow ever longer;
often one is as dazed as if drunk, and though repeatedly called back from this petty state, one utterly forgets this great matter—truly, this is sheer stupidity.

Safety and peril are summoned by one's own karma; calamity and fortune do not descend from Heaven. At the moment of death and physical decay, one’s appearance will not differ from that of a pig or a dog.

Myriad virtues are preceded by benevolence, and benevolence stands as the foremost of the Five Constant Virtues. Compassion dwells at the head of the myriad merits. How magnificent! In the discourse of the Three Teachings, though expressed with different mouths, they proclaim the same truth.
Every person cherishes their life; every creature craves its own survival. When a chicken sees the butcher seize it, it flies in alarm to perch before the table.
When a pig hears the price being called for its slaughter, two tears well up like a spring. Though the mind is originally clear and lucid, it is simply that the mouth finds it difficult to speak.

Suddenly one undergoes the agony of the butcher’s block; the bowels are severed, yet life still clings on. A thousand times the white blade slices through; one is boiled in the white-simmering cauldron of the red furnace.
The *pàoluò* torture is inflicted upon their body, while sweet meats and rich delicacies grace my table. If such deeds were not sinful, one need not fear the Azure Heaven.
From antiquity, the retribution of birth and death has revolved like a waterwheel. When I was in my early twenties, I witnessed these things with my own eyes and felt deep compassion.

I have gathered accounts from both ancient and modern times, nearly reaching ten thousand words, vowing to uproot the suffering of the three miserable realms; this resolve has grown ever firmer over time.

In this turbid age, you maintain a family of benevolence; may the blessings of the celestial palaces descend upon you. It has been heard that a single act of goodness can counteract an ill-starred planet, how much more so when such grace is extended to many lives!
Your ancestors strictly observed the precept against killing, and it is only through their example that you, their descendants, now possess such a model. Do not—
One regards trivial matters as insignificant; let us try listening to even a commoner’s words.
To celebrate, humans rejoice at encountering auspicious events; sentient beings weep and wail in sorrow. This humble body must surely be a guest enjoying the hospitality of its home. One.
A thousand times each night, one shivers with cold; who would have thought that karmic conditions would thus converge? Enemies pursue one another in succession.
Clad in fur and bearing horns, one remains silent; bowing the head, one is led before the blade.

The marriage of two clans brings together a new affinity; on this day of lifelong companionship, auspicious vapors gather thick within the courtyard. The abundance of delicacies—boiled, steamed, and roasted—is truly magnificent.
It is worth sighing that even among the species of birds and beasts, there is likewise the affection between husband and wife. It is only because...
In past lives, there was little compassion; today, they have come in pairs to fill the void of their destined end.

Their laughter and voices, their countenances, will never be seen again at funeral rites. Autumn frost and spring dew hold their sorrow; as fresh meat is struck upon the sacrificial platter, one gazes toward the soul’s return. May their merit increase.

Rather than accumulating further burdens through the bitterness of repeated deaths and rebirths, why not strictly uphold the Buddhist rites and reverently cultivate the Five Precepts and the Three Refuges?
That the deceased kin have not yet been delivered while your filial heart remains deficient—these words should be engraved within the five internal organs.
Regarding utensils, I observe that the vessels of Jambudvīpa, the insects of the blazing heavens, and all things are entirely subdued when a cold wind arises and turns them into emptiness.
This occurs before the severe frost and freezing have even set in; yet, as long as sentient beings still exist, their craving for life and fear of death are all the same. Do not say otherwise.
There is no merit in seeking rescue or protection; both great and small alike know pain.

To preserve the vital energy (*qi*) of the grains is sufficient to nourish the spirit; one should not consume excessive amounts of meat flavors. The myriad origins of disease originally enter through the mouth. This...
Those who are driven by greed do not understand this principle; they care only for their three-inch tongue, yet fail to consider their seven-foot body.
Truly pitiable and beyond pity, they bring suffering upon themselves and cause their wives and children to weep.
Regarding the superior matters of the heavens and the human realm, diligent cultivation of skillful means (*upāya*) must come first. Do not let this year pass by and wait for the next;

it is a pity that time flows on so imperceptibly. In all your daily activities, whether moving or still, you should contemplate how to provide for those who come after and bring glory to those who came before. Protect all living beings.
The method for this is fundamentally boundless; it lies solely in exerting oneself according to the occasion.
When birds and beasts face execution, their wailing and cries are most pitiable. With the frost-cold blade and boiling water before them, they are— [Fragmentary]
There is no way to settle this dispute; it seems he was in the world during his previous life and did not utter a single virtuous word from his mouth.
You have now witnessed this extraordinary injustice with your own eyes; when opening your mouth to speak, you must employ skillful means.

Exhorting others and restraining oneself, while feeling shame for one's own failings, is what makes one a true gentleman. Shun Yu contemplated doing good because he wished to share it with others; in setting his mind to save the world, he valued being magnanimous and broad-minded.

At every turn, he aimed to move and inspire others. If one relies merely on one’s own body and voice, it will be in vain—until the tongue is worn out and the ears go deaf—as people continue to influence one another [in such a manner].
To transform and guide others is easy to achieve merit. When the time is right for discourse, one may let things rest;

yet if one forcibly applies the principle of "extending empathy" (shang shu), it is like casting a finger into boiling water—the entire body feels as if it were being cut with knives. From of old, the retribution for killing is difficult to escape; ten thousand...
Amidst the turmoil of kalpas, responding to circumstances, a single thought may subtly stir the mechanism of killing;
one must courageously turn back to restrain it, practicing virtuous deeds with the urgency of hunger and thirst, gradually coming into accord with benevolence and compassion.
This confession is enough to startle the turbid world of Sahā. Ordinary beings are inverted and deluded; evil conditions blaze ever more fiercely while good conditions are faint.

Grief kills the eyes until their light falls to the ground. If one follows along with negligence and fails to repent in this life, there will be no time for repentance in future lives. One’s enemies...
Successive reports do not deviate; who has ever been seen to escape?

When the aspiration for enlightenment is aroused, the vast lands of the ten directions are none other than the all-encompassing measure of the nature. That sentient beings have not yet been delivered is my own fault. My hand—
Grasping the eight directions of heaven and earth, one must engage with the great assembly of humans and devas throughout many births and kalpas.
The two words "arousing the mind" are vast and boundless; within them, every Buddha is manifested.
Seeking a Swift Path to Rebirth. Zheng Chengde (Preface:

The people of this world suffer from the calamities of war. Such military disasters are all summoned by the karmic retribution of two layers of lethal deeds—those of the past and those of the present. Only by transforming the mechanism of killing through the mechanism of life can one turn misfortune into good fortune.)
The calamity of war exists within the human realm; it occurs perhaps once every several decades or several centuries, yet in the animal realm, it exists day after day.
The Way of Heaven favors life and abhors killing. Humans ought to refrain from slaughter and practice the release of living beings; do not, for the sake of food, set knives and blockades to work.

To exhaust one’s lifetime of merit and fortune, one slaughters the fish, shrimp, turtles, and turtles of the waters, and the beasts and birds that roam the forests—beings who share this world with us.
Within this same single mind, when life is taken, one must inevitably seek retribution.
To kill another in a past life was "me"; to be killed by another in this life is "him. Thus, in a state of topsy-turvy confusion, one becomes an enemy.
How can one’s mouth ever find release? It would be better for me to first refrain from killing; once a virtuous heart is stirred, its reach is boundless, and auspicious deities will attend.
Protecting one’s life is like being shielded by clouds and mists; it spares one from injuring the four great elements. When will the pursuit of life come to an end?
Through the reversal of causes and conditions, one becomes one’s own enemy. I urge people to rest early and now; through repentance, one can still save oneself.
I speak of releasing living beings and reciting the Buddha’s name; it is like a boat upon the bitter sea—able to provide refuge.
Diligently cultivate this Dharma yourself; it resolves the entanglements of resentment and leaves no fault behind.
In the past, there was a man surnamed Shen, who devoted himself to bestowing kindness upon aquatic creatures. He gathered treasures from the pond and obtained a golden basin;
gold and silver manifested from it inexhaustibly. A single sparrow brought him a ring to repay his virtue, and the Yang family enlarged their gate. All living beings [are thus sustained].
Those who carry a vital spirit possess the roots of enlightenment; do not harm these humble living beings.

There was also the True Man Simiao, who released fish and thereby saved a divine dragon; his medicinal prescriptions were passed down, widely manifesting merit and leading him to be certified as a member of the immortal ranks among the phoenixes and peacocks.
Most excellent is the old monk of the Lotus Pond, whose writings on releasing life and abstaining from killing are skillful; his every thought [is dedicated to this].
Dedicate these merits to rebirth in the Lotus Palace. Rebirth in the highest grade is honored;
the status of wealthy, noble, and divine beings in the Buddha-lands is all attained through the practice of abstaining from killing. Why, then, must we harbor further doubts?
Suffering arises from boundless karmic debts, and as war rages everywhere before our eyes, people flee east and west in misery—alas! Each person for themselves.
Quickly extinguish the heart of killing; thus you may preserve the peace and security of your person and family.

From the *Wèishēng jí* (Collection on Preserving Life), Maitreya Bodhisattva exhorts you to diligently practice the release of living beings; in the end, you shall naturally attain longevity. If you give rise to the bodhicitta, even great calamities will surely be saved by Heaven.
Furthermore, Lü Chūnyáng said:
"When your material possessions are about to perish, you must save them; when you yourself are about to die, Heaven will save you. There is no other method for prolonging life than this:
simply refrain from killing and release living beings."

Furthermore, when a finger is placed in a boiling stone jar, the whole body trembles as if it were about to burst; when a single needle pricks one’s own flesh, the entire body feels as if it were being sliced by knives.

A dying fish wails piteously toward people; a dying chicken cries out before the blade. Their lamentations are each distinct and clear, yet those who hear them do not recognize them for what they are.

Furthermore, although the practice of Master Shouguang of releasing living beings to prolong life may seem mundane, within it lies boundless merit from the unseen realm. In a single year, one accumulates a thousandfold blessings;
over ten years, one cultivates myriad layers of merit. For those already caught in the net and facing distress, or about to be cast into the boiling cauldrons and fires—
Startled and agitated, he encountered a pardon at the moment of execution—how immeasurable was that grace! May his life flourish, and may yours flourish as well.
Celebrate long life and refrain from killing;

for those on this yellow shore, human life is expected to reach a hundred years. When that time arrives, even the chickens and dogs will rejoice, as hearts of compassion fill the hall and they raise their cups in toast.
Guests: Drinking Blood and Eating Fur—Not Once Feeling Compassion.
Two Verses on the Precept Against Killing from the *Mirror of Compassionate Mind*, by Chan Master Cishou.

In this world, there is much killing of living beings; thus, the kalpa of weapons arises. Those who take life shall have their bodies slain; those who owe debts of wealth shall have their homes burned. You shall be separated from your wives and children;
for you once destroyed the nests of others, the retribution for each is exactly proportionate. Wash your ears and listen to the Buddha’s teaching.
When buying meat, it must be fatty; when buying fish, it must be alive; when buying clothes, they must be beautiful; when buying fields, they must be broad.
But if one is asked to buy life and set it free, not even a single hair is willing to be plucked. The road to the Yellow Springs is perilous; a misstep may make escape difficult.
A Poem on Abstinence from Killing by Bai Juyi:
All that lives upon land, in water, and in the void, Is held within the embrace of the Imperial Heaven.
If you were to imagine yourself wandering within a cauldron, Only then would you know the shock and terror endured by those of fragile bone.
Two Verses on Abstaining from Killing by Huang Shan-gu:
My own flesh and the flesh of sentient beings differ in name but not in substance. Originally they share the same nature; they are merely different physical forms.

Suffering is received from others, yet we crave rich and savory foods for ourselves. Do not wait for King Yama to pass judgment; examine yourself and see how you truly fare. I urge you to desist from killing life;
instead, you turn your back on them and give rise to anger. By eating their flesh, you will in turn be eaten by them; they will follow you like a ring around your neck as your master.
A Poem on Abstinence from Killing May Master Yuanyun’s verse endure for a thousand or ten thousand years:
The soup in one’s bowl has been stained by slaughter for ages past; The grievance is as deep as the sea, its resentment hard to appease.
If you wish to know of the calamities of war upon this world, Simply listen to the sounds at the butcher’s gate in the dead of night.
Again, Bai Xiangshan said:
"Who says the lives of all creatures are insignificant? They share the same flesh and bones, the same skin. I urge you not to strike the birds of the three spring months;
their young are still in the nest, looking for their mothers to return."
Furthermore, Lu Fangweng said:

"Flesh and blood dripping profusely—how precious its flavor may be! Yet such suffering is generally met with resentment that cannot be voiced. If one were to put oneself in another's place and touch it with the heart, who would be willing to take a knife and cut their own body?"
Regarding the colloquial words on abstaining from killing:

Great Master Yongming’s words are truly lamentable; human hearts are as hard as iron. Throughout the day you kill living beings and create karma. While it is their bodies that nourish yours, how can you bear this in your heart?
If, as a person, you encounter illness, you immediately go to kill and create karma. Do you wish for your own body [to be free from suffering]?
Peace and well-being. How could he be counted among those destined for calamity? Parents cherish their beloved child, yet they cause much harm to living beings.
While you, as a son, pray for your life to be prolonged, his own life cannot remain for even a single moment.

On the birthdays of parents, they slaughter pigs, sheep, and other creatures, wishing for their kin to live long and eternal lives; yet such a person ought to die and perish. Even the birds of prey and sparrows...
Among birds, beasts, tigers, wolves, and all such creatures, it is only humans in this world who are truly cruel. With bows and arrows, nets, and snares, they hunt;
yet among the aquatic species—field frogs, snails, slugs, yellow eels, black fish, loaches, and turtles—none clearly harm human beings. Why, then, do you take their lives with such bitterness?
Baring your teeth and grinding them together, you strike with a single blow, whereupon fresh blood flows instantly, boiling up like a cauldron.
Boiling water cleanses the woolen sweater until it is spotless; it guts, bellies, and carves out the heart, slicing the entire body into pieces.
Cooked and seared in a cauldron, seasoned with the five flavors to please the delicate tongue, once swallowed down the throat—three inches deep—one must ask:
what purity remains? Suddenly, the great deadline arrives; all delicacies are cast aside. When one reaches the Lord Yama...
Before the Hall, one sees only such vast karmic retribution: ahead, they are dragged and pulled; behind, they are pushed and hauled.
Every one is a life-threatening enemy; one cannot help but feel sorrowful and piteous. The entire body trembles with apprehension; the heart is filled with dread and fear.
The Judge of the Dead arrives to present the registers and ledgers, according to which their karmic offenses must be repaid. King Yama’s face is made of iron.

Sentient beings without emotion: struck through to the bone and blood by bronze hammers; subjected to ten thousand deaths and a thousand births in boiling brine; upon the mountain of blades, pierced by a thousand spears and cut by ten thousand knives;
fried in oil, sawn apart, and burned by fire; further drenched in boiling copper and hot iron.

Having endured every suffering of the hells, they await the issuance of a summons from King Yama, whereupon they emerge with their heads and faces changed—donning fur and horns to wander through kalpas, only to be slaughtered by swords and spears in their next lives.

They are butchered and slaughtered; upon death, they suffer the intense boiling of cauldrons and fire. Furthermore, they are treated like others who bite them, returning to them the karmic retribution of their own acts of killing.
They are transformed into oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep, born in the lands of barbarians where there is no clothing to cover the body and no grain or wheat to fill the stomach.
Though they long for delicious food and fine tea, they do not know when—by what year or month—they will exhaust all such various sufferings.

Having undergone such bitter suffering, one may finally be reborn in the heavenly Buddha-land and obtain a human body; yet, because many karmic offenses still remain, sores and abscesses frequently arise, with pus and blood flowing day and night.

Being ignorant of ritual propriety and the social constants, and disoriented regarding the cardinal directions, one further meets with a short life and a violent death—all of which is due to the failure to sever the heart of killing. One must instead take refuge with a sincere mind.

Regarding the Three Jewels, I have often encountered eminent monks who have transmitted their teachings. Having heard even a single word or half a phrase, I rely upon the merit of this Buddha-Dharma to sincerely and diligently uphold the Five Precepts.

With earnest and devoted aspiration for practice, if one’s single thought toward Amitābha is pure and true, Amitābha will personally come to welcome them to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, sparing them from creating further karma in the human realm.
*Pure Land Verses from the Western Studio* by Chan Master Chushi:
An inch of time is an inch of gold; I urge you to recite the Buddha’s name and quickly turn your heart back [to the Dharma].

Even if one holds the nobility of the Phoenix Pavilion and Dragon Tower, One cannot avoid the encroachment of crow-like skin and crane-like hair. Before the incense smoke within the cauldron has even dispersed, The celestial carriage in the void has already departed.
Beholding from afar, though every dust mote and every land is pure, it is only Amitābha’s vow-power that is profound.
Having left my hometown long ago, I speak of returning at last; why wait for your words? I know this myself. On the traveler's road, there is not a single thing of worth;
in human life, sorrow does not last long. My aging face appears clearly in the mirror, bringing grief; my white hair hangs in disarray, causing me shame.
Black stockings. Once again I read the "Eulogy on Nanying’s An-yang. The moonlight falling upon the roof beam reveals his elegant bearing;
he is a vessel of compassion floating upon the bitter sea of Saṃsāra. Can one transcend this shore and reach the other? To point directly at the source of delusion, one must recite the Buddha’s name.

Crossing the surging waves by a direct path, one avoids being swept away by the current. For thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas, may there always be peace and security; may all within the five destinies and three paths be brought to an end.
Cease and desist. Even if one’s own status is as low as the lowest grade, it is superior to being wealthy and noble in Jambudvīpa.
Of the hundred years of human life, seventy are rare; looking back upon past events, they are all seen as wrong. Every time I weep for my fellow beings, where have they gone?
They idly cast aside the Pure Land and do not think of returning. Fragrant clouds form before the emerald steps; numinous birds perch on coral trees.
Internally, as one flies toward the realization of the Dharmakāya, there is no illness or affliction; how much more so when feasting on the joy of *dhyāna*, forever forgetting hunger!

When speaking of impermanence, all matters seem trivial; eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty, one has no need for worldly toil. With a single mind, never retreating, contemplate the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*);
cultivate myriad virtues together, remembering Yongming. Thoroughly cleanse your prayer beads and replace the string; hold fast to the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
Cease your speech. Delusory conditions are exhausted, pursued only as flowers falling from the sky. Leisurely walk before the wind and beneath the moon. In a mere instant, youth turns to decay;
one must believe that impermanence urges on day and night. With the heterodox wisdom of the ninety-six schools, one undergoes saṃsāra for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
If you do not maintain the perception of the jeweled realm and its flower ponds, how can you avoid the mountain of knives and swords?
The tree has fallen; yet from a mind purified by itself, one gives rise to the aspiration and joy that here the noble ones permit one’s company.
By recollecting the Buddha, merit is profound and sins are naturally eliminated; the body returns to dwell within the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

There, the groves, trees, and grasses are joined with jade and crystal, while the great earth, mountains, and rivers unfold like brocade and embroidery. Once one has taken a step from this fragrant realm, precious lotuses spontaneously form beneath one’s feet.
The Flower of the Beginning: The jade-like brow-hair shines brilliantly upon the golden face; neither in heaven nor among men can anything compare to it.
Among gods and humans, there are none who do not witness his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); every single mark is identical in its golden hue.

He performs Buddha-works by scattering myriad wondrous flowers, causing fragrant breezes to arise throughout worlds as numerous as motes of dust and sands. When the light of his body touches their bodies, they become supple and soft; musical instruments and flowing sounds proclaim the Dharma.
Suffering and emptiness; leaning back against the carved balustrade, one gazes upon the jeweled trees. Boundless Buddha-lands are contained therein.
Upon the ground where he walks, every place is filled with rare treasures; strange grasses and numinous sprouts bring spring at every step.

Within these realms, there are originally no three evil paths; their adornments naturally include all devas and humans. The setting sun in the vast sky is like a suspended drum; the Great Sage is never without [this vision].
Manifesting his body, he has finally attained awakening only now after kalpas of vast eons; yet his native land was never separated from him by so much as a speck of dust.
Amidst the lotus flowers upon the pond stands the man above the flowers; the Buddha’s light shines upon his purple-golden body.

Hearing further the wondrous Dharma, he removes the defilements of the mind, saving all deluded beings to escape the wheel of suffering. With every step he travels through lands as numerous as motes of dust, fulfilling his vow to benefit living beings until the ultimate nirvana.
The time in the Sahā world is brief; how many kalpas of spring have passed in Sukhāvatī?
The Pure Land is truly an immortal realm, where one gazes upon the setting sun amidst clouds and mists. Pearl towers and jade palaces form its very substance;
emerald trees and golden flowers grow in dense rows. Gentle breezes sway the *kaṇṭaka* lotuses, while the lingering flowing waters carry their fragrance.
O Mandarin Ducks, you clearly remember the song of non-arising; I pray that you, who know the Way, will join me in a performance.
This body of ours is but a floating bubble, a dream, and an illusion—how can we simply indulge in greed and anger?

You should seek the direct path of cultivation; do not emulate those who are foolish and dissolute. Guarding the precepts is as pure as ice and snow; in governing the mind, one must strive to be equal to the sages.
Worthy kin, you have clearly pointed out the sun flying westward; may all who possess discernment reach the True Wood (Muzhen).
Time and again I dream of the House of Dharma; coming and going, the path is distinct and unerring. Pearl banners emerge from the water like the sun and moon;
jeweled canopies arrayed in the void resemble clouds and mists. A pair of mandarin ducks bathe together in the golden pond; two parrots hold jade [fruit] in their beaks.
Tree blossoms; sleeping in deep beauty, unaware of who has awakened me. A single incense burner’s fragrance drifts as the evening sun slants low.
Wind fills the jade terrace, water fills the pond; lotus flowers bloom branch after branch.

Listening closely to the calls of ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks—this is precisely the moment when body and mind are liberated. Necklaces naturally form of precious gems; the *kāṣāya* robe requires no effort at all.
The shuttle and thread of the Dharma: the Tathāgata’s marks and signs are inexhaustible to behold; the gates of illumination attained, I vow to maintain them all in total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
Pointing afar toward my hometown beyond the setting sun, a single path of return is as straight as a bowstring.

In the void, melodies play every kind of music; upon the water, flowers bloom one by one like lotuses. The branches and stems of various trees become a hundred jewels; the dwellings and sustenance of the multitude are most excellent.
O Devas, may my Master grant his grace and accept me; let not fifty years of arduous devotion be in vain. One lotus bud contains one holy embryo;
when a lifetime’s merit is perfected, a flower blooms. Necklaces befitting the body appear according to the mind;
vessels brimming with *sudhā* arrive with every thought. The golden hall radiates light that swallows sun and moon; the jade towers have no space to contain [the splendor].
Dust and grime! The Dharma King has discoursed upon the True Reality for me, until the very void itself laughs with cheeks full of joy.
The palace of the Jewel King and the gardens of jade; the places where one sits, lies, and walks are all of gold.

From time to time, the śarīra emits wondrous sounds; the kalaviṅka birds clearly play celestial melodies. By turning back the hearing, one suddenly awakens to the principle of non-birth; it is eternally abiding, omnipresent, and perfect.
When the mind moves, everything that meets the eye becomes a pure land. From kalpas past until the present day, I have established causes and conditions within these pure lands;
thus, they manifest before me throughout the two-and-six periods of the day. As each evening arrives, my wholesome thoughts increase, following the setting sun as it descends into the vast heavens.
May the Tathāgata’s precious hand personally touch the crown of my head, and may the Great Being’s golden body [embrace me].
Patting [his] shoulder: Without relying on a womb, this illusory form is formed; within our own house, there is naturally the lotus of the Jade Pond.
Lofty and majestic throughout the land, it is the sole Treasure King; neither morning nor evening does it fail to radiate auspicious light.

The *nyagrodha* tree bears fruits of pure gold; the *utpala* flower has chambers of soft jade. Its essence is self-evident and luminous, not dependent on the sun or moon; one knows that spring abides forever.
Frost and ice. Again, having returned from wandering through Buddha-fields, one gains heavenly blossoms that fill the sleeves with fragrance.
About to attend the Dharma assembly and pay homage to the Golden Immortal, one gradually follows the fragrant breeze out from the precious lotus.

The light from the red *uṣṇīṣa* flows on inexhaustibly; the golden-purple body’s marks shine boundlessly. Layer upon layer, jeweled nets hang over the level ground; each and every flower pedestal connects [to the next].
The distant heavens; these rare events within the realms of all Buddhas are as clear as a bright mirror appearing before me.
The supreme purity causes the fruits of the human path to be perfected. The nature and habits of this Sahā world are transformed all at once.

Like fish escaping a dense net to roam the vast ocean, like geese avoiding a drawn bow to enter the distant sky, the cycle of coming and going in saṃsāra ceases from this point on. May the afflictions of birth and death no longer arise.
The ability to bind [the mind]—when there is no mind, this is true purity and peace. If there is defilement, how can one hope for the precious lotus?
"Mind itself is Buddha" cuts through a thousand differences; the teachings and Chan are of one family. When the fruit is realized, the infinite body is endowed with the marks and signs;
its radiance flows like unspeakably many Ganges sands. Its wondrous beauty in other realms can never rival it; how could its original vows not be profound and subtle?
Easy to boast of, yet in general, one must begin cultivation early; only then will one avoid being obstructed by karmic conditions at the moment of death.
Thirty-two sands of Ganges rivers to the west—there, in that land of sublime adornment, lies my home.

Use the Single Truth as the seed, and take the seven treasures entirely as lotus flowers. Loathe the sufferings of this life in Saha-world; do not let yourself fall into the realm of indolence hereafter.
The differences between worlds arise suddenly from the water of the mind; it is like the present interplay of light and shadow.

From the Buddha down to the ordinary person, everyone has personally spent kalpas cultivating their practice. How could a pure land be obtained by nature? The Great Way is not originally sought outside of things.
First, one awakens to the emptiness of form and leaves the sea of desire; afterwards, one adorns oneself with merit and wisdom to sail across [the ocean of birth and death].
The Compassionate Vessel: from the present until the past, it has always been thus. Having delivered all sentient beings, its vow does not cease.
Where can the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name be fully gathered? The water’s light is deep azure, the lotus flowers are crimson. The broad and long tongue covers the three thousand worlds;
the gate of purity opens to the twenty emptinesses. Cloud-nets connect in shimmering pearls; the wind-swept branches spontaneously play the jade music.
Linglong: Throughout my life, I have made no vow for the realm of immortals; from childhood, I have longed to return to the Palace of Ultimate Bliss.
How can the praises of the country of Susumati ever be exhausted? It is not the same as the Buddha-realms of other directions. A hundred flavors, both sweet and sour, forever fill my bowl;
with this body light and vigorous, I roam freely through space. Having attained the patience of non-arising at the very first thought, I am able to instruct those bound by fetters.
The power of life is unimpeded; records of rebirth from ancient times to the present have been passed down. Throughout worlds as numerous as dust motes and sands, the true wind is fanned.

It is heard that when cinnabar was refined in the golden cauldron, a single dose caused one to soar in wonder to the abode of the Jade Emperor. One’s light departure was like willow catkins drifting on the wind;

one’s beautiful countenance was like peach blossoms reflecting the sun. Moreover, having cultivated the pure karma of body and mind with such subtlety, one has further attained the vow of the Compassionate Honored One.
Apply your strength here; this is the peerless Dharma for long life. There is no need to boast of the ten volumes of the *Siddha-śāstra*.

With a single range of cloud-covered mountains and a single thatched hall, a single jar of pure water and a single burner of incense—the mind, having dissolved all thoughts, returns to thoughtlessness.
One’s daily recitation continues from sunrise to sunset. When the rain has passed, the red apricots are at their finest in spring; when the breeze is gentle, the white lotuses flourish in summer.
It is somewhat prolix. Suppose the fires of the kalpa burn a thousand worlds; my own family’s sacred site of practice remains unmoved.

Red lotuses constantly reflect as white lotuses bloom; only the golden lotus is not easily planted. If one can, in every thought-moment, leave behind turbidity, then birth after birth one shall emerge from the womb.
For now, rely on the magnificent new fruits of that land, yet go forth everywhere throughout other quarters to manifest [the Dharma].
The old roots and the task of planting the lotus are not slightly different; both stem originally from the mud. Ten thousand sutras and myriad treatises do not falsely point the way;
they all together indicate the single path to the West. Moment by moment, scrub and polish the impurities of the mind until pure;

from time to time, guard against the sprouts of the Way being scorched. Dwelling within the lotus, one naturally realizes the body is secure; once the fruit is attained, it must cause the earth [to flourish].
In vain do you labor to calculate the *jiǎzǐ* (sexagenary cycle); a great kalpa of this Sahā world passes in but a morning.
Recently, someone has returned from the Pure Land; at the heart of a pond, a single jade lotus has blossomed. Upon its calyx, his name is inscribed;
already before his physical body, he has formed a holy embryo (*garbha*). In the eternal bliss of Sukhāvatī there is no death, whereas in Jambudvīpa, one is most severely oppressed.
How pitiable! The Dharma King has specially bestowed his compassionate grace.

Sitting together upon the hundred-foot golden terrace, when the mind opens through the height of contemplation and one beholds the Buddha, the body naturally arrives at the emerald lotus pond. Through thousands of kalpas, the karmic offenses of the wheel of fire are purified;
from the jade trees, light radiates in tens of millions of branches. One never tires of the profound discourse with virtuous friends; the wondrous speech of the numinous birds is indeed [sublime].
Inconceivable! An achievement so perfectly fulfilled in a mere instant is yet called slow by the rushing torrent or the flashing lightning.
Under the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, how many lose their human form and regain it again? Myriad practices are not equal to cultivating pure deeds;
why, with a single mind, do you suffer to cling to the red dust of the world? The Dharma King’s vow is as weighty as a mountain; the lost son longs to return, his tears flowing.
Tears fall frequently. If you can turn the gaze back to contemplate your own nature, the hundred and eight bright pearls are all your family’s treasures.

Morning and evening, they dwell within the mind of the Way; year after year, they participate in the Buddha-work. Advancing steadily toward the realm of peace and bliss, one performs the six periods of morning worship at the palace of the Dharma King.
One does not weary of the black smoke of incense from the square robe; how could the sitting mat be an impediment to the hands?
Sweat is red. How many such as these remain among those who have left the household life? Clearly recognizing the true master, one gazes westward at the crimson clouds and the white sun’s orb;
looking up at the precious throne and the body of purple-gold. One realm is pure, and every realm is pure; ten recitations are sincere, and every thought is sincere.
Born in the city of Ultimate Bliss, one shall never regress; throughout the entirety of empty space, all is understood.
Free from dust, you have long since floated and submerged within the ocean of suffering; how fortunate you are now to be one who has reached the other shore!
Those born in this Sahā world are exceedingly ignorant and foolish, entangled by manifold sufferings and unable to contemplate the way out. While in this world, they possess no pure karma;
at the moment of death, how could there be a time of liberation? Though the hundreds of thousands of sutras constantly offer such exhortations, among billions of people, not even one...
Second, the knowledge [of the truth]: The Great Sage of Golden Arms is most precious; he came early and led me into the lotus pond. He taught that oral dharma and meditative mind do not differ;
blue, yellow, red, and white are all lotus flowers. If you wish to know that Buddhas and Patriarchs have no written words, cease studying like children counting the sands of the ocean.

When the high seat speaks of the profound mystery, it is as clear as a mirror; the number of ancients who attained the Way— (Note: The final phrase "古人得道數" (the number of ancients who attained the Way) appears to be an incomplete fragment or a reference to a specific enumeration, likely pointing toward the vastness of those who realized the path.)
Like sesame seeds, pure lands are scattered throughout the various sutras; it is not only in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Amitābha Buddha, the Great Physician King, receives people and leads them back to the land of immortality. Whatever he grasps with his hand is a wondrous medicine; whatever he sets forth on his tray is an extraordinary prescription.
Within a grain of millet, one does not perceive the vastness of heaven and earth; within a small jar, how could one know the passing of years?
The moon waxes; this very illness has no place of origin. All-pervasive feverish affliction becomes naturally cool and clear.
Sitting alone in leisure facing the west, holding a rosary in hand, one recites without forgetfulness.
The name of the Buddha can purify the mind-ground, and the tongue-root then emits the fragrance of lotus flowers. As the radiant sun reaches the mountain’s edge, shimmering gold floats everywhere.
The light within the chamber; at this moment, there is no other thought. May you be permitted to behold King Drumisvara in person.

Alas for the turbid and evil sentient beings! When will the fruit of the Bodhi path be perfected? It is said in general that the land is purified according to the mind, yet how can one resist the body and spirit being dragged by karma?
When the true sword is brandished, the vines fall from the tree; when the clouds of delusion are dispersed, the sun [appears].
The flowing heavens; the void is ultimately without obstruction. The Pure Land flows on, right before one’s eyes.
[From] Master Shandao’s Eight Verses on Nianfo:
"Gradually the skin becomes like chicken-skin and the hair like crane-feathers; the spirit cannot avoid becoming exhausted. Piteous are the aging eyes, growing dim and blurred, just as..."
Floating clouds shroud the moon; deluded thoughts arise with every passing moment. When will the greedy mind ever find rest? It is better to recite the Buddha’s name early on;
thus may you transcend the sea of suffering from this day forth.
Behold his gait, faltering and frail; his head and belly are like a winnowing basket or a mortar. How can he endure the long journey when his strength is exhausted?

As he climbs the heights, his feelings alone grow more intense. Stepping out the gate onto the distant road of a thousand li, leaning on his staff amidst clouds and mountains of ten thousand folds—it would be better to recite the Buddha’s name early, so as to quickly behold the compassionate countenance upon the precious throne.
Even if one’s hall were filled with gold and jade, and one were adorned with pearls, emeralds, fine silks, and elegant makeup;

even if one constantly sang and danced beneath the flowers and daily raised cups and goblets before the wine-vessel—though such infinite worldly pursuits may seem secure, in the end they cannot escape death. It is better to recite the Buddha's name early on;
thus, at the moment of death, one will surely proceed to the Western Pure Land.
Decay, old age, illness, and death are unavoidable; do not boast of your vigorous strength. How long can this rosy complexion last?
Before long, white hair will suddenly fill your mirror. When this finite time has run out, the executioner of impermanence will come to summon you.
It is better to recite the Buddha's name early and awaken to Amitābha’s own nature.
Though you may enjoy a thousand forms of happiness, and though you possess ten thousand kinds of skillful means, by what means can this body be made eternally secure?
In vain do you speak of the wondrous elixir of longevity; before long, form and spirit shall part. How could it be permitted to rest even for a moment?
It is better to recite the Buddha's name early on; only the Pure Land is true peace and joy.
Impermanence will inevitably arrive. How pitiable are the sentient beings of the triple world! It is as if they have entered a mountain of jewels, yet contentedly return empty-handed.

Amitābha’s entire being is revealed, and the Pure Land unfolds in every direction. It would be better to recite the Buddha's name early on, so that upon turning away from this life, one may sit upon a lotus throne.
There is only the path of practice; it truly arises from one's own mind. Without departing from present mindfulness, one suddenly eliminates the ignorance of kalpas.
Fools still cling to themselves; how can the turbid defilements be cleared away?
It is better to recite the Buddha's name early on, so that the fruit of the Bodhi path may be perfected.
Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. This mind, in every thought-moment, is the Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no other mind, and outside the mind there is no other Buddha.
Like the blowing away of ten-thousand-li white clouds, a single red sun surges forth. The jeweled trees and lotus ponds appear before one, beyond the capacity of words or writing to describe.
*Sahapu* (Endurance): A *Yujia'ao* (Fisherman’s Joy).
Listen well to the immeasurable sufferings of Sahapu; they cause even the wise to increase their sorrow and dread. A lifespan of a hundred years is like the morning dew. You must awaken to this:
birth and death are the same for both the poor and the rich. Green hair and rosy cheeks cannot be retained. O hero...
Where have all the heroes gone? Turning my head, I see the road beneath Mount Beimang. The setting sun sinks low; thousands upon thousands of crows fly past in the twilight.
When one hears of the immeasurable sufferings of this Sahā world, every thought and calculation only exhausts the bowels. Earth, water, fire, and wind vie with one another for dominance.
Failure. How can it be secure? In the end, it all turns to fine dust. A single pearl of the mind remains free from defilement;
before sound and after form, it is ever revealed. When the skull is shattered, there is no place to find it—unless one awakens. Thus did the Tathāgata’s golden mouth personally entrust it.
I have heard that the Sahā world is filled with immeasurable suffering; birth and death together act as the masters of saṃsāra.
The six thieves wield knives as their companions; they dwell together, never for a single moment departing one another.
The Deity of Merit and the Woman of Darkness—these two find it most difficult to meet. A wise host accepts neither; follow my words, and from this day forth, let them not come near again.

Ascending the gateways, I hear that the Sahā world has immeasurable suffering. They boast grandly of their own abundance while feeling ashamed of the poor and destitute—those who have no food, no clothing, and no shelter.
Their cauldrons hang suspended in the air; they look up and see the red sun at midday. There is only the celery by the mountain stream that can be boiled; it is yellow.

Sitting in the dusk, I listen to the whispers of my hungry bowels; of much grain, much gold, and many children—these shared joys and gatherings, when viewed closely, are all but the decrees of past lives.
I have heard that the Saha world is filled with immeasurable suffering; now the karmic debts come forward to be repaid, as thieves plunder one's wealth and the body is beset.
Captive, encountering wolves and tigers; inciting life to death through sorcery and practicing *wugu* (witchcraft). Slaves toil in hardship under cruel masters;

afflicted with black sores, white leprosy, deafness, and blindness. Living together with the ugly, the wicked, the ignorant, and the foolish—who will pity you? Arouse your mind and take refuge in the Compassionate Father.
*Jia'oa* (Yueyu Jia'oa) of the Western Land:
It is said that in the West there is immeasurable bliss; the Three Sages and Ten Holy Ones all rely upon it. I bow my head to Amitābha’s perfect awakening; I shall long study and learn.
Like rivers flowing to the sea, as dust accumulates to form a mountain. The Buddha-nature resides within one's person like a jade rough; it must be polished.
Relying on the diligent carving and polishing of a skilled artisan, both the ordinary and the holy are produced by the mind; they are difficult to depict.

Adorned with jeweled pedestals, precious thrones, and pearl necklaces, hear and speak of the immeasurable bliss of the Western Land. The Dharma King’s governance and transformation eliminate all evils; in heaven and among humans, there is originally no [suffering].
Separated yet intermingled, the holy and the ordinary are equal, all equally perfect in awakened enlightenment. One constantly beholds jeweled flowers falling from the void;

morning and evening one hears celestial music. Food, clothing, and shelter are provided spontaneously without effort. Fragrant terraces and pavilions extend everywhere throughout the realm, vast and spacious.
I have heard that in the West there is immeasurable bliss; those of ordinary, shallow wisdom find it difficult to fathom. Whatever one prays for or seeks, there is nothing not obtained.

Why labor to seek [worldly things]? Pearls, fine robes, exquisite delicacies, and golden palaces—where the ground is as level as the palm of a hand and vast beyond measure, where the water of eight virtues requires no digging, and where one may take refuge within the heart of a white lotus flower. The appointment for three lifetimes—how could it be otherwise now?
Lightly cast it aside. It is said that in the West there is immeasurable bliss; the Sovereign is none other than the Tathāgata. He does not establish the three luminaries nor the Five Peaks;
he has eliminated the ravines and gullies. Red clouds and purple mists eternally enshroud him. His forty-eight features of countenance flash with golden brilliance; his almsbowl—
Take of the exquisite flavors as you please; making a vow to be reborn there is the supreme strategy. One can only reproach those who are like drifting reeds upon the road of birth and death.
Listen to the talk of the infinite bliss of the Western Land; once one hears this wondrous Way, ordinary cognition is forgotten. Not a single character remains within the breast.
The legs. Truly a standard of dignity. Radiance pervades the world as the crimson sun blazes; the wings of the great鹏 bird spread wide, making the vast blue sea seem narrow.
Who could further inquire after the sparrow by the hedge? How many ordinary hairs and holy horns are there? All are cast aside. In every atom and every land, all return to non-attachment.
Exhortation to Practice Nianfo by Master Shandao:
Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken and the hair like that of a crane; look at how one’s gait grows faltering and unsteady.

Even if gold and jade fill the hall, one cannot avoid decay, infirmity, old age, and illness. No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may enjoy, impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the direct path—[Nianfo].
Cultivating practice, I simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.

These essential words on the Pure Land were written by Bai Juyi (Bai Letian) when he was seventy-one years old: "I no longer devote myself to composing poetry; reading scriptures strains my eyesight, and performing meritorious deeds I fear the toil and bustle."
How can one cross over with the eye of the heart? Recite "Amitābha" in a single voice. Walking, there is Amitābha; sitting, there is Amitābha.
Even if one is as busy as a rushing arrow, do not abandon Amitābha. The day grows dark and the road is long; my life has already been wasted.
Morning and evening, with a pure mind, simply recite the name of Amitābha. The realized person should laugh at me for having too much of Amitābha.
But what of the realized? And what of the un-realized? I universally exhort all beings in the Dharma-realm to together recite the name of Amitābha.
Master Mingben of Xingming Monastery said:
"The suffering of the Sahā world! The suffering of the Sahā world! Who can enumerate the sufferings of the Sahā world? Yet worldly people conversely take suffering to be pleasure."
Dwelling complacently within it, one loses what is essential; from within this leather-and-flesh sack, the head emerges. One nurtures the disease of ignorance until it becomes a malignant parasite;
suddenly, the three-inch breath ceases, and one is transformed into cold ashes buried in the soil below.

As one transmigrates through the five realms without a moment’s rest, one suffers misery for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes. O virtuous ones, why not recite the name of Amitābha early on and renounce [this world]?
This Sahā world is suffering;
the Western Land is blissful. The bliss of the West accords with one’s capacity for awakening. Its people and its land are entirely sublime.
There is no cold or heat, nor are there the three evil realms. Emerging from within the womb of a lotus flower, one hears the sound of the Dharma at that time, equal to that of the devas.
How joyful! The lapis lazuli ground is so pure as to be free from even the finest dust; pavilions are formed of gold, silver, jewels, and pearls;

transformed garments and food appear spontaneously in abundance; and one’s lifespan is immeasurable, beyond calculation. O virtuous ones, why not contemplate Amitābha early on and attain that bliss of the Western Land?

**A Poem Exhorting the Cultivation of the Pure Land by Xiuxiuzi** Xiuxiuzi attained the state of "resting in rest" and said: "When one attains rest, one simply rests. Why weary the spirit? Why worry? My reflection in the green water-lily reveals that the countenance easily ages;
it urges me on, for the daylight of the world is difficult to retain. A hundred years are not long—like dew upon the heart of a flower; ten thousand affairs are ever-changing—like the flow of water."
The face is like a bubble; it would be better to cultivate the Buddha-way while there is still time. Having fulfilled the conditions for Buddhahood, he journeyed westward.
He heard it said that in the West, all manner of wonders are contained: its boundless scenery surpasses that of Mount Penglai. Forests of trees surround the golden ground in seven tiers;
flowers bloom in four colors within the jeweled ponds. Auspicious birds spontaneously tune melodies beyond the heavens; fragrant steps retain no trace of rain.
In the midst of dust and grime, how many among those born from lotus calyxes have come from the single phrase of Amitābha?
Master Yunqi Ju, in his *Qulian*:
"Who among the multitudes in this Sahā world understands their suffering? When will the cycle of rebirth end? They are like fish seething in a cauldron; how much more so those in cages?"
The bird in the midst exhorts the people of the world: "Hasten to turn your hearts; it is well to return home.

Who among men understands the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss? There, all afflictions are forever severed, and one transcends even the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception—let alone the island of Penglai.
I exhort the people of the world: hasten to turn your hearts; it is well to return home."
The evening bell tolls in the clear night;

Great Master Rong was pained by the brevity of life in Jambudvīpa. He lamented that all the toil spent chasing fame and fortune was but self-exhaustion, sighing that the dream of Nangko is short and dawn comes again.
Youthful countenances age easily; do not boast of your youth. Do not linger in the splendor of the halls amidst the laughter of the crowd. Beware of delusion and confusion.

Inverted, one commits every kind of boundless sinful karma. How could one know that impermanence lurks in the shadows? It makes no distinction between dawn and dusk; in an instant, its summons arrives.
One should realize that the sea of suffering is vast and boundless; one must cultivate the Way early, lest one wait until buried in the wild weeds.
How enviable is the merit that transcends all! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the exquisite adornments are such that golden sand fills the ponds and lagoons;

*mandārava* flowers swirl and dance through the air on fragrant mornings. Exquisite incense drifts with the wind, and celestial music plays spontaneously. Ascending to the Precious Abode, every step is upon jade and crystal, far removed from the clamor of the dust.
Here, suffering and affliction are entirely extinguished. I pray that the great assembly will contemplate their native land, turn the light back to reflect within, and [extinguish] the fire.
Planting spiritual sprouts within, we arrive together upon the lotus pedestal; our names are loftily inscribed, forever wandering in eternal freedom.
Spring, summer, autumn, and winter—these four seasons:

the Song Emperor Renzong’s poem says, "The breeze blows through the green willows; peaches and plums all bloom in flower. Even the grass sprouts its shoots, and even the wood sprouts its shoots. The swing.

The noble ladies and courtiers rejoice; the commoners, husbands, and farmers suffer in the desolate outskirts. Reflecting deeply, let those who rejoice do so as they will, and let those who suffer do so as they will. From this day forward, I shall generously bestow clothing and abundantly offer food and tea; I shall quietly recite the name of Amitābha and prepare my own home, sighing over the transience of this floating life. There is a song for this. *Song of the Floating Life* I have lived through many years, yet I have not yet seen the Buddha’s face.
