Existence is but empty flowers; non-existence is but empty flowers. I only wish that I may quickly cultivate my way to the Ocean Assembly of Amitābha.
In the lotus ponds of the Pure Land, sitting is a lotus flower, and standing is a lotus flower.
The fragrant breeze blows upon the verdant grass; all things naturally flourish and harmonize. The silkworms are just now completing their work; the wheat is just now reaching maturity.
Those who find pleasure atop high towers are idle and dissolute youths; those who suffer torment along the roads are travelers and merchants.
Reflect deeply: both the pleasures and the torments shall become empty. From this day forward, accumulate some merit through the cultivation of wholesome karma.
Zhi: Prepare well for the journey ahead; diligently recite the name of Amitābha. Be ready for the moment of departure.

Sighing over this floating life—whether one has it or not, it is but a hollow name. I only wish that I may quickly cultivate my way to the ocean-like assembly of Amitābha and the lotus ponds of the Pure Land, where whether sitting or standing, I am free and unimpeded.
The golden wind blows through the yellow chrysanthemums; the bright moon is at its full orb. Flowers all wither; fruits all decay.
From the eastern wall, one hears the news of men marrying and women being wed; from the western wall, one again hears the clamor of gongs and cymbals filling the sky.
Reflecting deeply, I see that the present is in vain and the past is likewise in vain. From this day forward, I shall practice the Dharma extensively.
It is well. Form many virtuous karmic connections; quickly recite the name of Amitābha. Prepare for the coming year. Sigh over this floating life:

with it, there is not perfection; without it, there is not perfection. I only wish that I may soon cultivate my way to the ocean-like assembly of Amitābha and the lotus ponds of the Pure Land, where sitting is peaceful and standing is peaceful.
A north wind blows through the pines and cypresses; goose-feather snowflakes fly down. The grass withers, and the trees wither as well.
On this side, there is clamor and bustle—red stoves and warm chambers. On that side, there is desolation—straw mats and hempen robes.

Reflecting deeply, I see that both the wealthy and noble have their share of right and wrong, and the poor and humble have theirs as well. From this day forward, I shall steadfastly maintain my fasts.
Observe the precepts. Awaken slightly to the mysteries of Chan. Diligently recite the name of Amitābha. Prepare yourself for the summons.

Alas, this floating life—whether it exists or does not exist—is a source of sorrow and grief. I only wish that I might quickly cultivate my way to the Ocean Assembly of Amitābha and the Lotus Pond of the Pure Land, where there is radiance at dawn and radiance at dusk.
In the West, the One Great Master is extolled;
the Compassionate Father of the West is named Amitābha. He receives sentient beings into the nine grades of the lotus pond.
This shortcut Dharma gate is easy to reach, yet alas, many harbor self-doubt.
In the West, there is the joy of wealth and nobility, where all enjoyments appear before one according to one's heart's desire;
difficult for either heaven or humanity to rival, he sits majestically upon a purple-gold lotus.

Not far to the West, seek nothing else; take the single phrase "Amitābha" as your meditation topic. If you can maintain this throughout your life without other thoughts, you shall roam at will through the Buddha-land of the Lotus.

Exert yourselves with diligence in the West without delay; once fallen into the City of Doubt for five hundred years, the Great Sage will emit light to illuminate and shatter it, so that you may return once more to the Pure Land and pay homage to the Golden Immortal.
The shortcut to the Western Land surpasses Zen meditation; with one phrase of Amitābha, spur yourself on with haste.
Ten million *buddhakṣetras* away, you arrive in the snap of a finger—yet for others, it requires nothing but a firm mind within oneself.

The Master of Transformation in the West delivers those mired in delusion; through the Buddha’s sustaining power, the Way is easily accomplished. Letting go of all and proceeding directly leaves no divergent path;
one must clearly distinguish this very first step.
Return early to your native land in the West; human life is impermanent, lasting but a breath. Cherish this limited time of light;
if you waste this present life, it will be difficult to emerge from it again.
Hasten in the West and practice early; birth and death are impermanent and cannot be anticipated. The sunlight outside the window passes with a mere snap of the fingers;
for a human being, how much time can there truly be?
The great vows of the West shall be widely disseminated. Exert yourself well in even a single phrase of Amitābha. Let it be clear and distinct without interruption;
let every sound awaken the true master.
In this hymn to the Pure Land, Master Dumen possessed lofty talent and grand strategy;
his spirit was extraordinary. At any critical moment, he never acted in haste. He idly schemed amidst beating rain and striking wind;
his writings moved heaven and earth in vain. If the river of desire has not yet dried up, shallow waves must still be stirred.
Thesis: The Six-Character Amitābha has no footnotes; taking refuge in it is itself the Great Compassionate Vessel.
World-Warning Verse by Zhou Bhatara:
Failing to form auspicious bonds with the virtuous, One suffers daily from the burning toil of craving fame and profit. How could one know that gold and silver remain in this world?
"Treasure! Borrow this for you to look upon idly for several decades.
Furthermore, as the Great Master Shiwu said:

'When rain passes over the thatched eaves, the sun turns red; in an instant, the weather shifts from gloom to clarity—how much more so when it comes to life and death, which occur in the space of a breath!'"
Matters of the world: at dusk, one can hardly guarantee hearing the morning bell again.
I see people of this age busy day and night, extensively building houses and establishing estates and fields. Yet, in the end, not a single thing can they take with them;
only their skull remains to be buried on Mount Beimang.
Everyone hears and knows there is birth and death; why do you not practice cultivation early? The majestic Great Way no one reaches;
with eyes wide open and clear, they fall into the fiery pit.

To say that the practice of cultivation does not depend on being late is to say nothing at all; there may be another year ahead this year, but within the three realms of suffering, a single retribution lasts five thousand kalpas—when will you ever emerge from it?

While harboring thoughts of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, I heard that the Great Master of Daily Contemplation had clearly perceived the matters of the Western Paradise. This journey must rely upon auspicious conditions;
if one polishes the teachings until a single thought is as clear as a mirror, one need not fear that Amitābha will not appear before one.
How can one escape the cycle of birth and death? If this mind remains unawakened, all effort is in vain. Now, I shall no longer dream of saṃsāra;
I will simply traverse this single journey through the human realm.
I exhort you to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, O Great Master Udumbara:

the four marks of human existence cannot escape death; even in the heavens, how could one ever avoid the five signs of decline? It would be better to dwell in the lower grade of the nine lotus realms than to return to this floating world to undergo birth from a womb.
To achieve long life, one need not rely on the formulas of the immortals; to save oneself in times of emergency, one must turn to the prescriptions of the Sea-Island.
By relying upon the Lord Amitāyus, it becomes clear that this alone surpasses all other considerations.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the gate of transformation; how could it be restricted to cities or villages?
Even if those with wrong views should hear it, it will surely fall upon their sounds and enter their faculty of hearing.
In this verse for recollecting the Buddha, Great Master Duzhi says:
"The Buddha is within your heart; you must keep your eyes open. Do not cast him behind your head and fail to look upon him. To miss this moment would be a true failure.
If you wish to be like those of this very day, I fear it will be too late."
Furthermore, Master Duanyu sought what he knew in the north, south, east, and west; fearing his head, he recognized its reflection and fell entirely into delusion.
Even if one were to awaken to the affairs of before birth, one still requires Amitābha to serve as one’s guide.
Fix the mind on a single phrase of Amitābha; whether daily life is leisurely or busy, regardless of its extent.
Even if one does not attain wondrous enlightenment by the end of their days, this shall still enable them to depart from Saṃsāra with their karma remaining.

In the lyrics of the *Guiyuanjing* (Mirror of Returning to the Source), Dharma Master Zhida praised the fruit of upholding the sutras as most perfect and the efficacy of chanting the Name as foremost. Suddenly, the dusty mind was washed clean;
suddenly, the dusty mind was washed clean. Having cast off the mundane world and severed worldly ties, in an instant one strides high upon the golden path.
The Golden Steps. In an instant, one strides upon the golden steps, exalting one’s name and lineage, and sits loftily upon the golden lotus. One must know this:
the Amitābha of one's own nature must be invoked by oneself.
Layer upon layer of earnest exhortations and instructions; the profound and compassionate vows of Amitābha. Deep and vast is the sea of suffering; bound by the heavy chains of karmic debt.
Amidst clamor and noise, one wanders through saṃsāra a thousand times over. Hasten to board the vessel of rebirth in An-yang.

From time to time, I pay homage to the ancient Buddhas who look down with compassion. Far and wide, along the ancient path to the West, I dwell eternally within the Land of No-Birth to realize the true teaching.

I sigh over this single play-ground of Jambudvīpa; I laugh at foolish people who create delusive thoughts, busying themselves day and night over the mere tip of a snail’s horn or a speck of dung on a fly’s head.
Day after day, one is intoxicated in the flowery halls; night after night, one is infatuated with rouge-clad beauties. One thinks only that for a hundred years there shall be no ailment;
how could one know that in a mere instant the body will perish? Alas! Worldly affairs are like the morning dew or spring frost.
In a single moment of impermanence—*ya*!—a noble human form is submerged in the surging waves of the river of craving.

I sigh that the suffering of saṃsāra has not yet ended; fortunately, our Buddha extends the compassionate ferry. He explains in detail the adornments of the Pure Land, delivering the deluded masses from the fiery pit.
Within the five turbidities, there is much misery and desolation; the agony of the three evil paths is a sorrow too profound to describe.

May every single being return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī), sitting upright upon a lotus pedestal. Thus, for the sake of the multitude, I—[the narrator]—exclaim: (Aligned with the source structure, the final line "俺呵" indicates the speaker's personal resolve.)
How tragic! Proclaiming this with utmost fervor: Alas! How could Jambudvīpa ever be transformed into the Flower Treasury World?
In haste, this floating life is like a flash of lightning; how agonizing, this cycle of rebirth through a thousand turns! The waves surge on, the sea of suffering boundless.
Who among those single-minded would be willing to recite the name of Amitābha? Most pitiable, they are needlessly entangled by desire and lust. Impermanence...
The moment it arrives, I fear the kite string will snap; the four elements separate as myriad karmas entangle me. My grievances and offenses—ten thousand sufferings in the hells.
How anxious I am! I gaze with longing eyes toward the Compassionate Honored One of Sukhāvatī.

Like a shuttle through the months and years, one sighs at a hundred-year span entirely consumed by the vexations of flies and snails. The youthful vigor of old—by this day, both temples are thinning with white.
Merit and fame are but vainly peering into an ant’s hole; the affairs of the world are utterly like a dream of the deer or a banana tree.

Singing in delicate tones, dancing with slender waists—the fine furs and horses of the Five Tombs are now but a faint memory. There is no limit to impermanence; how can man escape it? All such luxury and splendor...
For a thousand ages, one has been companion to the weeds and thorns.
Alas! Fame and profit have exhausted the person. Joyfully, this very day, the other shore is suddenly reached. Listen to these words; their reality and meaning are all fundamentally wondrous.
Suddenly awakening, the heart’s orifice is cleared. From now on, one awakens from the "Yellow Millet Dream. As for sounds, colors, luxury, and splendor—
Erase it all with a single stroke; practice must begin early. Do not let that Old Man of Yama issue his summons. How truly lamentable!
Worldly people suffer for food and clothing, burning with the pursuit of profit and fame. Clinging to this threadbare, withered carcass, they dote on their beloved.
How could they know that one day the dream will end and the shadow vanish? How bitter it is! On the road to the Yellow Springs, one is left alone.
Sighing desolately, I look up and find nothing but weariness. My former elegance and noble spirit—having reached this point, they have yielded to nothing but a scene of sorrowful lamentation.
As the slanting sun sinks with the flowing waters, my anxiety deepens; the transmission of the lamp to return to the source cannot be found, remaining only a mirror for those lost on the path.
A lamp in a dark room; returning home is near. It is just like a potent medicine that dispels the nature of delusion. May this lamp be transmitted throughout the great earth without end;
I only pray that the gateway of the True Dharma may circulate widely, so that every person may enter the realm of the Lotus.
*Man Ting Fang* (Peony Pavilion), one chapter:

For over sixty years, the Layman Zhuangyan has spent his time in a fleeting spring dream. Upon awakening, he finds the yellow millet porridge already cooked. What fine splendor is there in these floating flowers and illusory shadows?
With cold eyes, he lightly pierces through them; he quickly turns over, snapping the silken tether. His children and grandchildren play on. From [here].
He performs his part; why need one wait for the final act? With a handful of thatch upon the green mountains, this is the livelihood of my remaining life.

Let us deliberate on nothing else, but simply pass the time according to conditions. Washing the bowl and burning incense, first send the mind back to Sukhāvatī, where one may roam at will beneath the cool and pure jeweled trees.
How truly lamentable! When turning the head to look back, the ocean of karma stretches vast and boundless.
Cherishing the Original Vow of the West, I yearn for the Land of Peace and Bliss;

the realm of suffering in this Sahā world shall never end. I vow to be reborn in Sukhāvatī to enjoy its leisurely ease, to behold the Compassionate Honored One face-to-face, and to personally hear his teachings.
May my parents be led to transcend the three realms together with me, and may I successively repay the four debts of gratitude and the three existences. Leaping from the cage...

The joy that arises is overflowing; dwelling in the Lotus Land is truly wondrous. Without leading others, one is free from illness and old age; without plowing or weaving, food and clothing are abundant.
There are no sun or moon; day and night are illuminated by the Buddha’s light. The four seasons are mild, and the weather is free from cold or heat.
The pavilions and towers are adorned with the seven treasures; celestial music resonates afar, and extraordinary fragrances swirl about. Within the ponds...
Lotus flowers of five colors bloom; within the groves dwell birds of every kind. The multitude of arhats serve as fellow practitioners of the Way, and all the supreme virtuous ones are one’s friends.
One flies with ease and wanders at will through the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. This is the water of merit.
With a single sip, the knots and obstructions within the chest were dissolved. From this point on, there were immeasurable dharma-gates for severing afflictions;
he investigated each one with profound mastery and resolved to deliver sentient beings from the ocean of suffering and achieve the path of Bodhi.

The Twelve Hours Verses by Huangfu Shifang At the hour of Yin (5–7 a.m.), at dawn, the daily Buddhist recitation takes place in the early morning. With just one *ke* (twenty-four minutes) of effort and ten invocations of the Name, one can transcend birth and death and emerge from the depths of samsara.
This rare Dharma is wondrous and difficult to discourse upon; rebirth [in the Pure Land] is entirely caused by faith. You are able to listen.
If you receive this without doubt, you are one who has received the prediction of enlightenment for many lifetimes.
When the sun rises in the hour of the Rabbit, the morning dew easily dries and people easily grow old. Try to reflect carefully upon your kin and friends;
how many before your very eyes are now buried in fragrant grass? If you wish to practice the Way, you must do so early. A single inch of time is a priceless treasure; do not let it pass in idleness.
If you are unwilling to recite the name of Amitābha, you will surely suffer in vain when the end comes.

When the sun rises high, one must choose a neighbor when moving from this human world; do not seek blessings and rewards from gods and men, for even at the end of life, it is difficult to avoid sinking back into the cycle of rebirth.
Whether born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven or becoming a Cakravartin King, such temporary pleasures are not the ultimate truth. I exhort you to recite [the name of Amitābha].
The Buddha seeks to go westward, forever becoming one who dwells in leisure and sovereignty.
At the hour of *yǔzhōng* (mid-morning), when the smoke of cooking rises everywhere at the time of eating, he eats his fill of rice to satisfy his hunger;

through his own cultivation and practice, he brings an end to birth and death. The child remembers the mother; the mother remembers the child. Ultimately, the entire effort rests with oneself. One must be willing to sacrifice the body.
In my heart I behold the King of Vows; though over a hundred thousand leagues away, he is as near as a span.
At midday, when the sun of the Buddha is at its zenith, my eyes do not gaze upon it. Along this single straight path, few people travel;

instead, I turn back toward the long road to undergo hardship and toil. I do not discuss Zen, nor do I wave the fly-whisk; in every thought-moment, Amitābha remains my constant Lord. Although my body...
Before leaving this Sahā world, the spirit has already found rest in the Lotus Land.

While the sun’s reflection remains, how many times have we entered and emerged from Jambudvīpa, sharing a single room with the six serpents—a sight truly worthy of dread? Through many lifetimes, we fail to distinguish between the clear and the turbid.
Turn your head sharply now and wash away the dust of worldly existence; human life is impermanent, and one must not avoid facing it—the character for "death" is ever-present.
Hanging just above the eyebrows, one suddenly perceives that the West has flavor.
At the hour of Shen (5–7 p.m.), sighing over the human body as being like a turning wheel: "If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life shall it be delivered?
Do not miss the opportunity; do not be complacent. How many beings wear horns or scales!"—the compassion of the thousand Buddhas.
Pitiful, they are difficult to save. For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have remained submerged and lost.

As the sun sets in the hour of You (the West), the lingering light of its reflection does not endure long. How laughable that fools look only to what is before their eyes! Do you know of this great matter of birth and death?
Stinking wealth and idle tea and wine cause ordinary people to run about all day long; rushing and bustling, they never rest.
Idle thoughts of Amitābha—when the days and months arrive, one stands empty-handed and helpless.
At the hour of the Dog (7–9 p.m.), a single lamp illuminates the night chamber; climbing into bed, one parts with socks and shoes.

Soul and dream are shrouded in darkness as black as lacquer. Alas for the human body, so easily lost! To escape the cycle of rebirth, one must recite the Buddha’s name; otherwise, boundless sins will follow.
Obstacles are momentarily dispelled; the Buddha’s light is as bright as a thousand wheels of the sun.
It is the hour of Ren (亥), when people are settled in their beds. Wealth, nobility, and fame do not endure forever; the dream of the yellow millet on the pillow has not yet awakened.

In one's deluded state, one still worries about a thousand years. To be merely negligent and fall into indolence—when a single breath ceases, there will be regret for kalpas beyond measure. One would have brought shame upon the West [the Western Paradise].
The King of Vows, now approaching old age, extends his golden arm from afar with grace like the ocean.

At the hour of the midnight rat, purity and defilement manifest their forms, distinguishing self from other. Were it not for the bitter afflictions of this Sahā world, who would be willing to extinguish the mind and weary of birth and death?
Having attained wearying detachment, one must know how to find rest; upon the ground of golden light, bliss is beyond compare. Before one’s eyes, all vexations—
For whom do afflictions arise? They are all messengers from the West urging one to prepare for the journey.
At the hour of the Cock (1–3 a.m.), if you wish to be reborn in the Pure Land, who would pull back your arm? It is precisely within the field of affliction that one should practice;

let your mind respond to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Free from right and wrong, beyond affirmation and denial—let all matters follow conditions; what have I to do with them? Simply gaze upon the lotus.
The lotus does not grow on land; its roots are firmly established in the mud.
How magnificent is the gateway to the Pure Land! It is both supremely simple and supremely easy. By upholding the Name and aspiring for rebirth, there is no one who does not achieve their goal.

Yet, those of us with the faculties of ordinary beings have shallow capacities; thus, doubts arise in turn. First, we doubt our own long-accumulated habits, thinking that past karma is difficult to cast off.

Furthermore, I fear that my power of mindfulness is feeble and unable to reach the sublime realm. I do not realize that from time immemorial, the nature of sin has been fundamentally illusory and false.
One need only hold the name of the Buddha to swiftly extinguish the sins of birth and death, just as the wind sweeps away clouds and mist, or as a lamp dispels darkness and obscurity.

Dark clouds are fundamentally not real; when the mind is empty, it washes away all accumulated defilements. How much more so these names of the ten thousand virtues—their responsive resonance is inconceivable.
Like a stone whose nature is to sink, once it finds a boat, it will never fall. Like a person who has committed an offense against the law, the imperial grace can grant pardon and protection.
The power of the Buddha is wondrous and inconceivable; one’s own power is likewise extraordinary. Do not say that the power of mindfulness is slight;

the power of mindfulness will surely accord with one's wishes. Mindfulness is firmer than metal or stone; mindfulness is sharper than a blade. If you mindfully direct your thoughts toward the West, you will certainly be reborn in the West. If you practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, the Buddha will certainly come.
The maxims of the former sages are such that even a commoner finds it difficult to alter their resolve.

Those of the Two Vehicles perceive only partial emptiness; clinging to principle while abandoning phenomena, they consequently claim there is no Pure Land. [Yet] the meaning is that when the mind is pure, the land is pure.
One does not know that mind and land are neither one nor two. All lands arise solely from the mind; within a single mind, all sentient beings are complete.
Pure Land is the purity of the mind; Saha World is the defilement of the mind. If Pure Land is but a hollow name, then Saha World must likewise be a fabrication.

Through the measure of one's love, one is born in the Sahā world. With focused mindfulness, one departs from the West. Since pure and impure states arise within the mind, the land likewise corresponds to what is bestowed.
It is like the single wheel of the moon reflected within various waters: when the water is clear, the moon is bright; when the water is turbid, the moon is obscured.
The moon is compared to the primordial mind; the waters are compared to all worlds. A single mind contains ten thousand lands; do not interpret this in terms of existence or non-existence.
It is neither real nor unreal; both phenomena and principle are free from entanglement.
The Complete Works of the Ancestor Lü:
The Family Treasure of the Immortal of Pure Yang. Shi Tian [Surname], of Yangzhou, by nature delights in reciting the Buddha’s name, doing so daily without ceasing.
Once, while traveling to Huqiu, he reached the summit, where there was a quiet chamber enshrining an image of the Ancestor Lü; from the lintel hung a single wooden brush.
Beneath the branch was a sand-tray supported by a stand, upon which sat an old man. Shiqun asked, "What is this for?
The old man replied, "Whenever there is a matter of doubt, I use talismans and incantations to petition on behalf of others; when the Patriarch descends here, he will naturally pass judgment.
Shiqun silently bowed and wondered whether his constant mindfulness of the Buddha would have any efficacy. After a short while, a wooden brush suddenly—
Yet it moves spontaneously. He made a single judgment, saying at length: "At the end, he inscribed: 'The Immortal of Pure Yang (Chunyang Daoren) presents this to Tianji of Shizi in Yangzhou.

Wearing awakening upon one's person—sincere mindfulness of the Buddha is itself the elixir. Rotate the hundred-and-eight beads in a cycle; when mindfulness is perfected, one transcends birth as a śarīra.'"

Death: Contemplate the bonds of Bodhi to discern the holy from the mundane. Let your contemplative mind not follow the flowing stream; let your contemplative heart always accompany the white clouds in leisure.
Through contemplation, open the wondrous aperture to penetrate spiritual wisdom. I now leave this verse for you to contemplate.
A seven-day period of silence for the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) without self-assertion:
take seven days as the limit and do not seek [the Dharma] elsewhere. Face west and recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing. Time passes so easily that it is truly to be lamented;
if honored guests arrive at the door, forgive them if you cannot respond.
To achieve samādhi and be born early within the lotus, one must first sever external conditions. Speaking of right and wrong increases distraction;
therefore, for seven days, do not open your mouth to speak.
Set a fixed time to observe silence and recite the name of Amitābha; sternly exhort body and mind, never letting them stray. The ocean of suffering is deep and vast, difficult to cross alone;
I pray to rely on the Buddha’s power to escape Saṃsāra.
The karmic conditions of my transgressions are truly lamentable; I have repeatedly encountered the calamities of war and fire.
I vow from this life forth to escape birth and death, silently and single-mindedly seeking the Great King of Vows.
Universal Exhortation to Mindfulness of the Buddha:
In the West there is a Buddha named Amitābha, Who receives and guides sentient beings out of the River of Affection. All Buddhas proclaim this together;
you should believe it with earnest attention, So that at the end of life you may avoid seeing King Yama.
It does not matter if you do not awaken to the mysteries of Chan; it is enough simply to focus your mind on reciting the Dharma King’s name.
Provided that you attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī at the moment of death, you will suddenly open to the Buddha-wisdom, wondrous and immeasurable.
Not being versed in the sutras, yet reciting the name of Amitābha, is superior to possessing great erudition and wisdom. The six characters of the Great Name are the true Dharma-realm;
they universally encompass the ocean of teachings, free from all confusion and error.
If you wish to depart from the realm of birth, death, old age, and sickness, you must seek the Great Compassionate King of the Buddha-land. Amitābha is originally our true father;
reflect on returning home early, never forgetting for even a moment.
The Compassionate Father of the Land of Bliss gazes upon Sahā with longing; for ten kalpas he has extended his hand with earnest solicitude.
If you truly desire to transcend this sea of suffering with this very body, from this moment forth, quickly and swiftly recite the name of Amitābha.

How fortunate, how fortunate, truly fortunate! The gates of the Vows of Dharmākara open wide; even the most wicked and foolish person who can recite the Buddha’s name shall be escorted to the purple-golden platform at the moment of death.

Truly, I restrain my human emotions and feel ashamed of my verbal transgressions, wishing to cease my speech; yet I fear I may fail those who share my heart in the practice of *nien-fo*. In the afternoon, I shall speak briefly of the matters of birth and death;
as for worldly right and wrong or long and short, let not your lips be opened.
Time passes swiftly and life is hard to preserve; day by day one must guard against entering the gate of death. When guests arrive, do not speak of worldly affairs;
you should recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing the sound.

The physical body is a hollow deception and a profound source of resentment; though one employs a hundred schemes to arrange it, all efforts are in vain. The mutual encroachment of old age and sickness is especially fearsome;
at the time of death, the body swells and its stench permeates the heavens.
In these verses on the Pure Land, Chan Master Sanfeng does not disparage Chan, Vinaya, or the masters of the sutras; moment by moment he directs his mind toward the Western Paradise in this manner.
Having cast off all states of attachment and aversion within the Dharma, a lotus naturally emerges from the pool of the pure mind.
At evening I hear the village wailing; at night I hear songs. The affairs of the world are unreliable and subject to many transformations.
When both song and wailing are forgotten, the mind is naturally pure—there is only this single phrase: the Ancient Amitābha.
A single note of the bamboo flute rests upon the ox’s shoulder; the grass turns from green to yellow as the year passes.
Having herded this inch of mind back to the Pure Land, the white ox has no nose and requires no leading.

Worldly affairs are crowded and bustling, yet old age does not cease them; with white hair flowing and fluttering, one still rushes about in pursuit. When dwelling in the shade, the body and its shadow rest together;
the single phrase "Amitābha" is the ultimate realization.

If, for a single day, one truly severs [delusions] from before and after, one will not think of them again for the rest of one's life; this is what is meant by "correspondence. At the moment of death, there is no need to wait for others to come to one's aid;
naturally, lotus flowers will welcome one from beneath one's feet.
From the *Lotus School Treasure Mirror* (*Lianzong baojian*), Bai Juyi [prays]: "In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, there are no evil realms nor any sufferings.
I vow that those like my own self, aged and infirm, shall be reborn together with me in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha."
From the *Wenlei of the Land of Bliss*, "Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in Peaceful Nurturing":

Master Yongming [Zhiyue] [on] Amitābha’s Precious Realm. The auspicious name of "Peaceful Nurturing" (An-yang) resides within the land of retribution; it is the ultimate bliss and the most pure among the ten directions.

Through the twenty-eight gates of contemplation, one enters the profound stillness by cultivating meditative concentration; through the forty great vows, one directs the distracted mind toward rebirth by transformation.

Thus, throughout one's entire life, one upholds [the teachings], and for a single lifetime, one takes refuge. Immortals ride upon clouds to listen to the Dharma, and beings in the void sing hymns in praise.
Upon the purple-golden terrace, one ascends in person, proving that the original vow was not in vain; within the white jade tuft of light, the spirit...

Transformed, they become single-minded and rejoice within themselves. Consider the praise of the broad and long tongue: it is proclaimed simultaneously throughout ten lands. It merely indicates the mind so that all may be in accord;
it is not a hollow transmission based on mere whim. The axis of the earth turns, celestial flowers scatter before one, and in a single thought-moment, the blossoms open.
Upon seeing the Buddha, all attain the wondrous fruits; a thousandfold radiance shines forth. Realizing the Dharma, they all rank among the former sages.

Examining the past and inferring the present, those who have attained rebirth are not few. When the time comes, celestial music fills the void; when the moment arrives, extraordinary fragrances pervade the chamber.

Within this realm of singular truth, although these manifestations rely upon the Buddha’s majestic power, the scenes beheld within the pools of the seven treasures all arise from [the merit of the practitioners].

The mind emerges; thus we know that the Sage’s intent is unfathomable and his responsive resonance is enduring. He transforms the mundane into the sacred in an instant, and clarifies delusion into awakening in a flash.
Having unearthed the immortal scriptures, these are truly the arts of longevity; they point the way back to the Pure Land.

They dwell eternally in the land of the deathless. Furthermore, there are world-transcending sages and Great Beings dwelling amidst the dust of the mundane world who, as an act of practice, burn their bodies and kindle their arms;

they suspend their stomachs or hold their hearts aloft to establish the standard for others. They do not follow when celestial music comes to welcome them, nor do they rejoice when divine youths request their lives.
Whether amidst the blazing fires atop mountain peaks or within the mirror of radiant light, they have forever ceased hearing even the name of the evil realms.

Casting aside the baseness of the womb-hell, one’s eyes open and one’s tongue is fixed as proof is established; the ox-charge and the chicken-scoop suddenly cease, and while dwelling within the Iron City, one resists the King’s decree.
One must follow one’s sincere heart; seated upon the Lotus Throne, one relies on the Buddha’s grace, finding it difficult to abandon the ultimate truth.
Should one happen to slander the Triple Gem or violate the precepts, then at the moment when the winds and knives force the body apart, one shall face the retribution of karma.

While looking at his reflection in a mirror, he suddenly encountered a spiritual friend who manifested a wondrous forest of swords transformed into seven rows of jeweled trees, and turned a chariot of fire into a lotus pond of eight virtues.
The hells dissolved away; in profound stillness, his fear completely subsided.

Celestial flowers flew down to welcome him, and in an instant, a transformation Buddha appeared to greet him. His wisdom-eye became clear and his mind enlightened; the incense burner fell from his hand as he responded.
The lotus did not wither when the prophecy was given, yet the Jewel Forest did not endure long after the prediction was received. How marvelous! The power of the Buddha is inconceivable;
it has never been seen before in the past or present. This concludes the "Fourfold Examination of Chan and Pure Land."
If one has meditative concentration but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray; when the realm of the subtle body manifests, they are instantly carried away by it.
If one has no meditative concentration but possesses the Pure Land, ten thousand who practice, ten thousand shall go; once one has seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
To have both Chan and the Pure Land is like a tiger with horns; one becomes a teacher of men in the present life and a Buddha or Patriarch in the future.
To have neither Chan nor the Pure Land is to face the iron bed and copper pillars; for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there will be no one to rely upon.
In praise of Chan Master Yongming Yijue: Layman Li Ji of West Lake drew the Pure Land lots seven times;
throughout his life he never regressed and practiced with refined diligence. His spirit now dwells in An-yang, for which I have composed this verse.
It is worthy that his compassionate countenance be hung within the Nine Shades.
Verses for Painting an Image of Amitābha Buddha (with Preface). By the Layman Dongpo Su Shi and the Vinaya Master Yuanzhao of Qiantang.
These are universally exhorted to both monastics and laypeople to turn their sincere devotion toward the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

Su Shi of Meishan respectfully donates the hairpins and earrings—the legacy of his deceased mother, Lady Cheng, the Grand Mistress of Shu Commandery—to commission the artisan Hu Xi to paint an image of Amitābha Buddha, in order to dedicate merit for her posthumous welfare. He expresses this with a verse:
The Buddha, with his great perfect enlightenment, fills the worlds of the ten directions. Yet, due to my inverted perceptions, I have drifted in and out of birth and death.
How can I, by means of a single thought-moment, attain rebirth in the Pure Land? I have created karma since beginningless time; even a single thought-moment contains more than enough.
Since they arise from a single thought-moment, they likewise perish within a single thought-moment. At the place where arising and perishing are utterly extinguished, I am identical with the Buddha.

Master Baimu of Saha-duḥkha, whose disciples delight in contemplation, spoke these words of exhortation. Now, I shall add [these] six verses on "The Suffering of Saha" to the collection, wishing that they may be shared with others.

Sharing this with fellow sufferers in the Sahā world, we endure suffering through long kalpas of saṃsāra. Without severing the causes of suffering, we depart from the burning house only to follow karmic retribution into the womb once more.
We have betrayed this spiritual citadel; morning follows evening, and the cycles of cold and heat press on in haste—a single illusory body.
How many days can this last? A hundredfold illusions and deceptions roll up the dust;
how can one emerge from them? The suffering of *saṃsāra*—one’s life and body are but a drifting water-plant. Insects struggle for petty gain upon the eye of a gnat;

snails steal empty fame upon the horns of a cow. A single spark of resentment is hard to settle; the conflict between self and others flourishes, and ignorance grows day and night. At the very end of hell...
They enter in groups; in the West, there is no one willing to practice. They die in vain and are born again in vain—the suffering of Saha world.
Emotional thoughts rush like the wind; within the village of the six thieves, there is not a moment’s rest. Within the casket of the four serpents, they further attack one another. Who is the master?
Lacking the power of wisdom, one is caught in the revolving cage of the net of craving, turning ever toward the four corners.
Stumbling along the ground, I do not think of my two feet as they tread upon the void; the path ahead grows ever more hurried. Alas for the suffering of this Sahā world:
birth, old age, sickness, and impermanence. From the nine apertures flow stench and filth; within this leather sack is stored a mass of pus and blood.
Striving for the weak, striving for the strong—following deluded thoughts, indulging in desire, one becomes even more reckless. One must recite the Buddha’s name and contemplate the sutras.
They say that clinging to signs is permissible; breaking the fast and violating the precepts cause no harm.

I only fear King Yama and the sufferings of this Sahā world. All day long one wanders through the dusty realm, unaware that the years follow the flowing water. How can one bear the white hair replacing the youthful complexion?
One turns in the cycle of the six realms at will—ancient or modern, who would dare to be idle before death? Perilous and fragile are wealth and fame.

As soon as one grasps it, empty vanity, wealth, and beauty come to pursue and entangle. Honor and disgrace last but a moment; this *saṃsāra* is suffering. Light and shadow pass as swiftly as a flowing stream.
When will the cycle of favor and insult, sorrow and joy, ever end? When will the disputes of right and wrong, and the delusions of self and other, cease?
The road of birth and death stretches on and on—within the three realms, like a single bubble upon the water. Even for a hero...
His merit covers the world; yet he leaves behind but bleached bones buried in a desolate mound.
How could this compare to turning back one's head early? A Verse for Laywoman Chen (with Preface):
When Laywoman Chen saw Master Cibian, the Master asked how long she had been practicing cultivation. The laywoman replied that she had practiced for many years. The Master asked:
"Who have you seen? Ba called out. "I have seen many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). The Master asked, "How did they instruct you?
He replied, "They point directly to the source; they neither study the scriptures nor recite the Buddha's name. The Master said, "That is mistaken."
Because he preached the Dharma, Vāṣpa was moved to faith and understanding. Thereupon, [the Master] showed him two verses:
"Directly cutting through to the source, there is no need for cultivation; Considered from this perspective, such talk lacks foundation. One must grasp the root to escape birth and death;
In every thought-moment, invoke Amitābha—do not seek elsewhere."
Reciting the Buddha’s name and reading the sutras are one's fundamental practice. One must believe that from the beginning, water has always been ice. Simply investigate deeply at the source;
with every utterance, it will be raised with perfect clarity.

Verses on Exhorting the Cultivation of Pure Practice The Vinaya Master of Great Wisdom heard it said that the Western Land is the most easily sought; from this moment, ten thousand conditions shall cease at once.
With prayer beads in hand and feet crossed upon a round mat, he does nothing but serve as the pedestal for Amitābha.
Verses on Exhorting Others to Mindfulness of the Buddha, with an Explanation by Vinaya Master Qingzhao:

Śākyamuni Buddha truly praises the Western Land; The transcendence of both the primary and secondary realms is clearly manifest. With faith, vows, and the holding of the name, free from other thoughts, With every sound, the mind dwells within the light of the white tuft between the brows.
The four-character sublime name was proclaimed from the Golden Mouth; success is achieved solely through the firmness of one's own mind. This divine method is simple and truly rare;
once liberated, one joyfully dwells upon the precious lotus.
Verses on the Essential Points of Mindfulness of the Buddha (With Preface) By Dharma Master Cao’an.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata taught that Amitābha Buddha is the Body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya*).

Furthermore, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi stated that the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is its essence. Relying upon these two teachings as the essential points of the mind, [one realizes that] even across ten million billion lands...
As if gazing into a clear mirror, I have composed this humble verse to seal my own mind. Should there be any who understand it, might they rejoice in it?
The boundless oceans of lands encompass emptiness; that ocean and emptiness are entirely the Lotus Palace. The Lotus Palace pervades everywhere throughout emptiness.
The Ocean: Within the ocean of emptiness, the countenance of Amitābha alone is revealed. Amitābha Buddha is neither born nor extinguished;

like the moon in water, he is difficult to find and difficult to grasp. This body is utterly beyond words of separation; such is its resonance, and such is its teaching. I and Amitābha are fundamentally not two;
it is only through the latent arising of deluded perception that they suddenly become distinct. From this day forward, I shall sweep away all dust of emptiness and existence. Father and Son, Heaven.

Yet, as we have met one another, we vow to cultivate the three merits and diligently practice the six recollections, ensuring that our actions of body, speech, and mind remain free from flaw or blemish.
Now, by means of this mindfulness of Amitābha, I shall never grow weary until I behold him.
Verses on Exhorting the World to Practice Buddha-Recitation:
What is the nature of life in this fleeting world? It is like a spring swallow building its nest. In a state of restless toil, one labors to provide for a household;
It would be better to recite the name of Amitābha according to one's capacity.

With brilliant prose and eloquent debate, one may attain a high rank; clad in crimson and purple, one’s personage flourishes with great spirit. Yet, who among those of high office can avoid the arrival of impermanence?
It is better to skillfully recite the name of Amitābha.

Flying spears and swift archery are difficult to withstand; A fine steed gallops by as fast as a shuttle. Though one’s strength may rival ten thousand men, it fails in the face of old age and illness;
It is better to cultivate wholesome thoughts of Amitābha.

Wealth and possessions one never tires of accumulating; from morning till night, one calculates them, fearing even the slightest error. Unaware of one’s own distress, the hair on one's head turns white like snow.
It is better to be content and mindful of Amitābha.
With a clear and resonant voice, one may excel at singing; a single verse of new lyrics may be harmonious in its meter and tone.
Even if one’s singing could cause the drifting clouds to fall, it would not equal the purity of reciting the name of Amitābha with a cleansed mouth.
With willow-leaf brows and star-like eyes, she vies with the Goddess Xiang’e; her jade body is ever adorned in fresh silks and brocades. Such radiant beauty may endure for but a few more years;
it would be better to recite the name of Amitābha at once.
In chess, one boasts of many strategies against rival nations; in the game of capture and retreat, one vies for precedence in refining skill. Half of one’s life is thus wasted on these pursuits;
it would be better to sit upright and recite the name of Amitābha.
The merchant broker is most restless, traveling everywhere to distant lands and foreign regions.
Amidst the perils of wind and waves upon rivers and lakes, it is better to return home and recite the name of Amitābha.
They are accustomed to exploiting and ruining others; they craftily stage lawsuits and flaunt their henchmen. As family wealth gradually dissipates, they incur the resentment of others.
It is better to avoid such troubles and recite the name of Amitābha.
The karmic debts of your murderous deeds have gradually accumulated; with what words or reasoning will you face King Yama? I shall teach you a method for transcending rebirth on this path:
it is better to recognize your remorse and recite the name of Amitābha.
A Poem on Longing for the Native Land of An-yang, by Dharma Master Luan’an:
The Western Pure Land is originally my own home; Now I recall the journey back, a hundred thousand miles away. Wandering the roads of exile, I am utterly exhausted;
Isolated and suffering amidst the dust and wind, I am most pitiable. Seven tiers of trees tower high with a thousand delights; Eight virtues fill the deep pools—four...
Flowers of form. Do not be surprised that my dreams of home have grown so intense lately; alas, matters of honor and disgrace are boundless.
In years past, it was easy to leave the jade tower; originally, I had no intention of traveling far. Who would have thought that now my hair hangs white as snow?

My single-minded longing remains suspended like the moon on its western hook. Upon my pillow, I must endure the sound of the "bird thinking of returning," while outside the railing, I am frequently startled by falling [leaves].
Autumn Leaves. A stick of sandalwood incense smoke, a single strike of the chime— Casually gazing afar, tears flow down my cheeks.
In "A Poem on Yearning for the Western Land," Master Kemi has already known that the present is right;
what could be wrong with the past? I close my thatched gate fast as the sun sinks toward its setting glow. The tips of the bamboo sway gently in the new moonlight.
Above, the middle of the curtain is half-rolled as the evening clouds depart. The essence of mountain and forest fills my breast; the fragrance of pine and cypress permeates my robes.
Upon a flat stone and a lotus-cushion, I sit in perpetual meditation; with a single thought, I fly westward after the setting glow.
Pointing west toward Aparagoyānī, and further still to the west, lies the Jetavana Monastery. There, lotus blossoms open their calyxes with light that never fades by night;

the ground is spread with lapis lazuli, its brilliance utterly free of mire. The wind stirs the sound of the Dharma, surpassing the eight melodies of the sages; the pools flow with waters of virtue, excelling the dual streams of the Twin Rivers.
If, at the end of life, one but attains rebirth there, one shall follow the nine grades of the teaching, descending as low as one’s station.
A Historical Verse on the Pure Land by the Layman of West Lake, Li Jinenren:

The Buddha manifests a defiled world to take in the Sahā realm; He employs many skillful means to subdue and gather the stubborn and strong. There is no other method for crossing the river of craving directly;
He teaches only that one should single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha.
From antiquity to the present, the waves of vast eons surge; the two wheels turn in alternation as swiftly as a shuttle.
Cycling through the six realms without rest, how can one fail to seek the Western Return? Alas, what is to be done?
Verses on Cherishing the Pure Land by Chan Master Mingben:

In reciting the Buddha’s name, one must expect to reach the ultimate end; When that end is reached, both the name and the recitation are withdrawn together. The winds and waves of the bitter sea of Saṃsāra are stilled;
One sails steadily upon the red-lotus boat to the Land of Bliss.

People ask about the affairs of the five desires, which are boundless; the shackles of profit and the fetters of fame are so strong they cannot be severed. If one takes this mind of profit and fame and recites the Buddha’s name, why need one toil in hardship waiting for the future?
Out of attachment and views, you gave rise to greed and anger, burying your sixteen-foot golden body. Today, by good fortune, you have returned to the Pure Land;
you should not continue as before to stir up dust and wind.
To plant the nine grades of lotuses of the Western Land throughout the entire three-thousandfold world system of this defiled realm—upon careful reflection, there is no other method;
it requires nothing more than a single thought of firm resolve.
Seven layers of dense, covering pearl nets; three tiers of flat, spread agate steps. The Guide of An-yang’s compassionate vows are earnest;
from afar he extends his golden arm to receive those who come.

I send word to the people of this Sahā world: if you seek the path home, do not be complacent. Once you have pierced through the silver mountains and iron walls, the thousand-petaled lotus shall be a springtime all its own.
The moment one wishes to return home, one arrives at home; why need one pointlessly give rise to sighs of lament? The great road before the gate is as straight as a bowstring;
should one attempt to traverse it through thought, one immediately goes astray.
In the past, Śrīkṣetra attended upon the Buddhas of Sun and Moon Light; they instructed him to maintain mindfulness and direct his thoughts toward the Western Quarter.
Since personally realizing samādhi, he has never been apart from the side of the Compassionate Honored One.
At dawn and at dusk, I perform repentance and prostrations; bowing my head and weeping, I address the Venerable Amitābha: "How many times have I wandered through the six realms of rebirth?
I vow that this time, I shall escape the snare."
In old age, reciting the Buddha’s name is most fitting; with few days remaining, do not forget it for even a moment.
The six characters, "Namo Amitābha," are called the compassionate vessel that crosses the sea of suffering.
Everyone says it is difficult for the young to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; I say that youth is precisely the right time.
Behold the Dragon King’s daughter at the age of eight, who held a divine pearl in her palm that radiated precious light.
In harmony with Yuanming’s “Return Home,” and following Deacon Feng Jia’s “Return Home”:

The Lotus Society has already been established; why not return? Reflecting that my years are daily approaching decline, and considering how worldly conditions are truly lamentable, I contemplate the traces left at Donglin and find there the sages of old to follow. Seizing what remains of my life...
I still remain here, repenting of my errors prior to the age of sixty, like one who brushes his cap after a fresh wash, or like one who shakes out his robes after bathing.

Having washed away the dust and grime to hasten toward purity, I seek the subtle and profound mysteries of the wondrous Way. Looking back upon the path ahead, my heart turns toward it with the urgency of a galloping horse.
Entering the chamber of compassion and ascending the gate of liberation, the myriad realms are simultaneously stilled and the single truth alone remains.
Incense fills the burner and pure water overflows the vessel; gazing toward the West, one cultivates contemplation and prays to swiftly behold the compassionate countenance.

Entering the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, one experiences the lightness and ease of body and mind, transcending the highest grade of the nine lotus realms and closing the dark gates of the six destinies.
Concentrate the spirit in right meditative absorption (*samādhi*), closing off the ears and eyes from superficial observation. Wait until this retribution is exhausted;
then point directly toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss and return straightaway. Walk in meditation beneath the jewel trees, linger amidst the flower gardens, and then depart—*guīqùlái xī*.
One can only roam within the Pure Land. Contemplating the turbidity and evil of Jambudvīpa, why would one abandon this land to seek elsewhere?

Rejoicing in the immeasurable length of one’s lifespan, what cause for suffering or anxiety could there ever be? One meets with those of supreme goodness and takes the Bodhisattva who is to succeed [the Buddha] as a companion.
The ponds are composed of the seven treasures, with boats made of gold; the ground is spread evenly with lapis lazuli, devoid of any unevenness.

to give rise to further doubt is sheer stupidity.
The Western Land is precisely the land of Mind-only. If you do not recognize the West, how can you recognize the Mind? You, Disciple, mistakenly hope for a perfect and sudden understanding;

The West is precisely the land of Mind-Only; to attempt to negate the West would contradict the underlying principle. A single speck of dust in Sukhāvatī is equal to the ocean of lands;

The Western Quarter is precisely the land of Mind-Only; do not misrepresent the essential intent of Mind-Only. Delusion and awakening, going and coming, are fundamentally the hidden nature;

The West is precisely the land of Mind-Only. The Sun of Wisdom hangs high for those of the foremost capacity. When phenomena and principle are fused as one, this is the truly pure karma.

If one says, "I do not now seek birth in that [Pure Land], nor do I dwell here; being unattached to both, I shall accept rebirth according to my will," this is even more unreasonable. Why? Because you are neither a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body nor a Sage of Responsive Transformation;

since craving for existence has not been eliminated and karmic conditions have not been severed, if you are not born in the Western Land, you will certainly be born in this world. Once born in this world, you remain within saṃsāra; dragged by the power of karma, you have a share in the three miserable realms.

How then could you accept rebirth according to your will? To forget both the pure and the defiled is itself a dust-mote of the mind. This single thought of forgetting both purity and defilement is still a mental calculation; it still belongs to what is categorized as *dharmaviṣaya* (mental objects). If one truly forgets both, then what obstacle would there be to seeking birth? Birth.
Fundamentally, there is no arising of the four lands; even seeing is free from seeing when one sees the three bodies. One must know that the true and the delusive are originally of the same essence;
delusion and enlightenment have always depended entirely upon the person.

As soon as one is exhorted to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, they claim it is "clinging to signs. Yet, when they contemplate their own greed and attachment, they remain muddled and deluded. While there is ultimately no birth, there is nonetheless birth.

(For those who hold to the view of annihilationism, claiming that after death there is eternal extinction and no place of rebirth at all—they fail to realize that karma drags the consciousness along, which ultimately enters a womb once more; apart from the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land, there is no other way to escape.

To claim freedom from signs while still dwelling within the midst of signs—(if one says that because there is eternal extinction after death, one need not seek rebirth, and thus this is "not clinging to signs"—then one has departed from the signs of dependent origination and given rise to the sign of nihilistic annihilation. Annihilation...)

"Characteristics" refers to the dharma of false views; only when mindfulness merges with the Buddha is it truly "suchness" (*jì*). Jingxi said: "Because their essence is non-dual, it is only then called 'suchness. The intelligent people of recent times all say 'the mind is itself the Buddha,' yet when they are urged to practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection), they immediately claim it is 'attachment to characteristics.

They do not realize that the recollection of the Buddha and the recollection of the mind are originally one body. If one clings only to the recollection of the mind and does not recollect the Buddha, then the mind and the Buddha are two; how can this be called 'suchness'? When the mind differs from the object, one does not know emptiness.

To manifest principle through phenomena is called 'true emptiness'; to negate phenomena in search of principle is called 'perverted emptiness' (*pāpaka-śūnyatā*). The intelligent scholars of recent times also know that the mind is pure and the land is pure."

To speak of the Pure Land and immediately say that one is "attached to signs" is to fail to realize that there is no land outside the mind and no mind outside the land. If one merely clings to the doctrine of "mind-only" while disbelieving in the Pure Land, then mind and land are split into two; this is a "wrongly grasped emptiness," not true emptiness.
One must first believe in the Buddha’s teaching of the mutual non-duality [of mind and land], after which the sun will shine upon the mountains and rivers, and all places will be interconnected.
It is universally said that the Pure Land is solely the mind; the journey of over one hundred thousand *yojana* is but seeking externally.

To cling merely to the deluded mind as residing within—(if one claims that the West, a hundred trillion Buddha-lands away, is external seeking, then one recognizes the deluded mind within the square inch of the heart; this is identical to one of the seven positions reckoned by Ānanda)—is to remain ignorant that the essence of true nature encompasses all.

(The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "You should know that empty space arises within your own mind, like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so the various worlds within that empty space? Amitābha.
The Buddhas are reflections in a mirror; Sukhāvatī and Sahā are bubbles upon the water. Whether grasping or rejecting, loathing or delighting, there is no obstruction;

one may wander freely within the house of one's own home. (Because one delights in the purity of one's own mind, one grasps; because one loathes the defilement of one's own mind, one rejects. In this single grasping and single rejecting, there is no hindrance to the Mind-Only—what "external" could there be?)
It is said everywhere that every place is the Western Land; level plains and high mountains all offer no hindrance. When entering the latrine, how could one still stop up the nose?
Why, when rushing through the mud, does one still lift the hem of one’s robe? Having fallen ill, how can the mind remain free from suffering?
In a dream, who knows the body is upon the bed? Do not speak empty words that contradict actual practice; it is better to rely on the setting sun to gaze toward home.
Cease speaking of the hardships of rebirth in Sukhāvatī; to say it is difficult to attain is itself a gate of obstruction.

The Buddha’s power can naturally eliminate the force of karma; with the root of faith, one may uproot the root of doubt. It is like deeply evading a private debt only to encounter official punishment, yet meeting with imperial grace.
Morning and evening we shall follow you, packed for the journey; in this life, I shall never fail the Compassionate Honored One.

Do not cling to the *Dharmapada Sūtra* while rejecting the Pure Land; the patriarch’s wondrous function and the Buddha’s words are both perfectly interfused. By means of words, the principle is recommended to manifest our teaching;

by attaining the meaning, one forgets the words to reveal the fundamental school. When the ten virtues are cultivated together, how could one commit transgression? When the multitude of sages assemble, who would remain in ignorance?
Whether in other lands or this world, what coming and going is there? The Dharma-realm is luminously present before one's eyes.

Do not disdain the abundance of delusive thoughts when reciting the Buddha’s name. Observe instead from where these delusive thoughts arise. To attempt to gather and restrain them with no mind is surely a sickness;
to intentionally strive to dispel them is likewise a demon. It is like trying to extinguish a fire while carrying firewood, or digging a breach in a dike to let water flow into a great river.
You must recite each syllable with utter clarity. When recitation reaches its limit and emotions are forgotten, what remains?
If you wish to achieve uninterrupted practice, you must apply yourself with diligence for it to truly correspond [to the Way].

A moment’s loss of mindfulness is like clouds obscuring the sun; a fleeting arising of thought is like smoke smothering a lamp. A small stream flowing long enough will eventually pierce through rock; boiling water, if the fire is extinguished, will also turn to ice.
Rebirth in the Pure Land and the attainment of Buddhahood are not remote matters; they depend solely upon the power of one's own mindfulness.
When walking, maintain right mindfulness of Amitābha; with every step, follow one Buddha as you pass. Underfoot, you constantly roam the Pure Land;
in every thought within your heart, sever ties to Saṃsāra. When passing willows or flowers, you must look back; by water or mountain, do not let him go.
Once you have attained rebirth in Sukhāvatī, you may come and go throughout the ten directions as you please.

The heterodox paths meet at a fork where the mind is one; they compose their own scriptures and establish their fundamental tenets—(namely, that the present five schools and six volumes of all such heterodox traditions have stolen from the Buddhist sutras, intermingling them with vulgar language to form their own canons).
At the side of the two-fold gate, secret instructions are transmitted; in the village of three families, the multitudes gather.

Mong! The path to the Land of Bliss is originally level and straight; the Buddha-dharma is impartial by nature and fundamentally most equitable. I exhort you to turn back and return to the True Teaching;
with every thought of Amitābha, you shall perceive the True Emptiness.
In this world of suffering, there are only those who suffer. Having created new calamities for oneself, what can be done? Wild weeds cover the ground where spring does not reach;

with one’s body bound in shackles and chains, the night is hard to pass. To cry out in grievance, do not call upon Heaven or Earth; when crying out in pain, you ought instead to contemplate [the Dharma].
Buddha! The three realms have always been a prison; I urge you to leave this Sahā world as soon as possible.

Do not take pleasure in the profusion of worldly delights, for when joy reaches its peak, sorrow inevitably follows. Though the city is filled with flowers and willows and one carries a beautiful companion...
Guest: Throughout the night, lutes and songs have intoxicated us in this painted tower; we perceive only the wine upon our faces, yet who knows that death lies at our very heels?
The Western Pure Land is truly a place of bliss; simply recite the name of Amitābha, and you shall travel there to roam.
The leisurely person reciting the Buddha’s name enjoys true ease; do not let your time pass in vain. Old age brings letters with white hair;
death leaves no official decree, and life cannot be retained. Prepare your provisions in advance while you still have the body; do not worry for your children before your own eyes.
The woman was sorrowful. "It would be well for you to return home to the Land of Bliss; there, clothing and food are provided naturally, so there is no need to plan for them.

I urge you in haste to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, for you cannot find leisure. By the time you have leisure, illness will have appeared before you. When the mind falls into disorder, you must apply yourself."

The Eye: When mindfulness arises from a state of busyness, one must apply the whip. Entering alone with a single blade into a thousand armies; passing a spoonful of water into a hundred-boiling cauldron.
The Buddha is not hindered by busyness; it is one’s own self that is hindered. Therefore, from this very day, I shall serve the Golden Immortal.
In my declining years, the passing moments are painfully few; like a flash of lightning or a bubble on water, they last but an instant. As yellow leaves gradually wither, I am truly old;

the autumn wind is about to arrive—what can be done against this sorrow? Without artifice, do not greedily cling to this floating world; if you have a mouth, you should do nothing but contemplate the Dharma.
Buddha! Farewell; as you depart, you must exert yourself. Do not allow yourself to waste ten thousand kalpas.
Sickness upon sickness is itself the remedy; know deeply that birth and death are impermanent. Having endured heavy punishments, one suffers in the prison of sorrow.

In the hells, intense suffering constantly oppresses this skin-sack; moment by moment, contemplate Amitābha and cease turning your back on awakening. Thought after thought, aspire for Sukhāvatī and wish to return home.
When shall I attain a pure and ethereal body, with a lifespan as immeasurable as the sands of the Ganges?

At the time of death, do not needlessly panic. (For those who recite the Buddha’s name, the first thing to avoid is the fear of death. If one fears death, one will not attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

There are many who recite the Buddha’s name throughout their lives, yet at the moment of death they focus solely on taking medicine and seeking physicians, never mentioning the matter of rebirth. This is the fault of fearing death. It disturbs right mindfulness. If one’s principles are clear during ordinary times, one will not err when the critical moment arrives. With earnest mindfulness, turn [the mind] toward [the Pure Land].

In that realm, the bag of skin is gradually discarded along with pus and blood; the foul-smelling, tattered garments are about to be cast off. The many afflictions of birth are truly a grievous malady;
Amitābha’s single phrase is the King of Medicines. In this deep and bottomless sea of suffering, one need only seek deliverance; do not worry that the Buddha will not launch his compassionate vessel.
First, bound by the causes of karma within this Sahā world, one undergoes many births and transmigrations, truly bitter and painful. In an instant one leaves a house only to enter another;
swiftly one discards a body only to receive another. One has once been a king or nobleman contending for kingdoms and cities;
how often has one perished like an ant in a speck of dust! If one does not contemplate returning now, one will continue as before to suffer through the cycle of rebirth.
The Gate of Vows of the Compassionate Father Amitābha has opened; he gathers in all sentient beings as if they were his only child.

From amidst the mass of pus and blood, one is freed from foul impurities; within the fragrance of the lotus, one receives a womb. Rely solely upon pure vows as your excellent guide; only doubt is the discarded material.
This turbid and evil Sahā world is difficult to dwell in for long; quickly join with virtuous friends to compose the song of returning home.
The Verse on the Eight Sufferings:
Driven by the winds of karma at birth, consciousness enters the womb; hidden deep within the prison gates, it is truly pitiable. Whenever it encounters hunger and emptiness, it hangs upside down.

Below. Frequently startled by the sound of coarse food pressing down from the mountain, the Śrāvakas reached this place with minds still obscured; the Bodhisattvas therein had not yet opened their wisdom.
Vowing to sever the ties of affection, they were born in Sukhāvatī; from within a lotus flower, they emerged as jade infants.

In old age, I am surpassed in all things; others have already retired from the world. My physical form brings shame, for it lacks the vigor of youth. Once my rosy complexion has vanished, it leaves no trace;
my new white hair gradually turns to frost. Shedding tears, I secretly recall the joys of childhood; seeing others, I can only speak of my own prime in vain.
My years grow old; who would know that the spring of the Pure Land remains forever? I shall not allow my body and mind to be busily occupied day and night.
When the four elements fall temporarily out of harmony, this body has no means by which it can be arranged. Like a fading lamp leaving but a shadow, it cannot be sustained.
A Dream: Night rain drips with sorrow as the empty air fills the streets. Where have all past joys and pleasures gone? Who now can harbor this bitter pain?
How could one know that the body of ultimate bliss is pure and void, Wandering freely upon the white jade steps?

The consciousness of the dying spirit is about to end, suddenly overcome by impermanence. The four elements separate, difficult to control; like a tortoise shedding its shell, the pain is utterly absolute;
like a crab falling into boiling water, one is filled with frantic terror. Willingly accepting the prison gates as companions, one stands with hands bound at the dark barrier.
The Ghost-Jade: How could it compare to personally beholding the Buddha as the flowers bloom? Without birth or death, his lifespan is immeasurable.

The sorrow of parting from those one loves, and the separation from life and death, is most pitiable; every mention of it makes one’s heart ache to break. [This concludes] the Farewell to Xiang Yu within the Lady Yu’s Tent.
Feathers flutter as the Princess of Bing bows on horseback to thank the Sovereign. Her tears are deeper than the rivers and seas, yet she still deems them shallow;
her resentment extends beyond heaven and earth, yet she feels it not yet long enough. May all those of supreme goodness gather in one place, and may they never be parted throughout vast eons.
When meeting those one hates, all people’s hearts desire to flee; who would have known that past karma summons them together? With wealth, it is hard to buy the pardon of the Lord of Yama;
with no stratagem, one cannot seek leniency from the wardens of hell. Zhang Xun, defeated in battle, thought of becoming a ghost; Xiao Shi, when her life ended, wished—
I have become a cat; when shall I be permitted to join the assembly at the Lotus Pond? Let the enmities accumulated over kalpas be extinguished together.

In seeking what one cannot obtain, whether in poverty or success, there is always a cause from former lives. The more one harbors hope, the more one becomes negligent; though I raise my sails, I repeatedly see my vessel sink.

Guest: Hanging up the placard especially grieves those who have failed their examinations; though they till the soil and plow for a lifetime, it is hard to fill their bellies. Though they spin and weave year after year, they still wear robes of coarse cloth like hanging quails.
In the Land of Bliss, clothing and food are naturally excellent; there is no need for such petty toil and bitterness.

The five aggregates (pañca-skandha)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are in a state of blazing intensity. Form refers to the body and all material things; the other four aggregates refer to the mind.
"Blazing" means fierce and violent.
Oppressed by these many painful matters, there is no place for one’s lamentations; where the liver and entrails are severed, emotions are difficult to sustain.

Severed. When the blood and tears have withered, my resentment has not yet withered. Having served as an envoy for twenty years by the sea, a single night passing through the pass has turned my hair white.
When shall I cultivate meditative contemplation in the Pure Land, where quiescence and illumination arise simultaneously, transcending both existence and non-existence?

The practice of sprinkling water from a bag to protect living beings is the most difficult of expedient means; one should cultivate these subtle practices without being lax toward oneself. Life and its essence have always been without distinction of size;
death and birth are the points where they intersect. If even a single hair removed from the body is known to cause pain, how could filling the belly with a full cup of wine not do so?
Endure hunger. I earnestly exhort practitioners to be meticulous. Every morning, one must diligently inspect the water for insects.
Preface to the *Jingye Tang Shi* (Poems from the Hall of Pure Practice):
In the third month of spring in the year of Gengxu, I confined my feet in the western courtyard, to the right side, of Fantian Temple. [The Inscription]...
In his room, he would receive honored guests for a brief meal of incense. Upon meeting, they would exchange only a few words of spiritual discourse.
Aside from this moment of incense, he did nothing but recite the Buddha’s name. He composed a poem to manifest his resolve and addressed the assembly, saying:
The Provincial Governor sold his property to build a Chan hall; the ancient temple once again opens its Pure Practice Hall.

Sweeping away all myriad attachments as if they were spittle and saliva, he relies upon these four characters as his provisions for the journey. Fellow practitioners together form a three-year community; when facing guests, there remains but an inch of incense.
The samādhi is not yet perfected and the practice is not yet matured; this body shall never again enter the city walls.
Spontaneously composed:
Being incompetent, I ought to dwell only in the deep mountains. My single chamber is desolate as I alone close the gate. Send word to the people of the world:
do not summon me; this life shall never again reach the human realm.
With this rosary of one hundred and eight beads and the Six-Syllable Sutra, I have spent my years and passed my time. Throughout my life, I have had only the vow to return to the West;
how could I bear to betray this heart for the sake of other attachments?
To rescue those drowning with a shattered boat is logically impossible; one must row with all one's might until reaching the shore.
Once the oarsman has helped them onto land, to move again to a new boat and enter the middle of the stream once more—what purpose would that serve?
A Song for Awakening the World by Master Hanshan:
In the red dust and white waves of the world, all is vast and boundless. Patience and gentleness are the wondrous remedy. Go everywhere as conditions permit to prolong your years;
Throughout your life, maintain your station to pass the time. Do not let the field of your own mind grow dark; Do not speak of the faults of others.
Lose your reputation; be prudent in social dealings so as to avoid regret. Endure vexation when performing tasks; it is better to deliberate before acting. A stiff bowstring always snaps first;
I have often seen that a hard sword-blade is easily wounded. Misfortune is brought about solely by idle talk; one incurs blame because of a hot temper.
There is no need to dispute right and wrong or argue over self and others; why must we judge each other’s strengths and weaknesses? Deceitful flattery...
Greed and hatred are the true hells; impartiality and integrity are heaven. The musk deer dies first because its scent is heavy;
the silkworm perishes early because its silk is abundant. The world has always been full of defects; how can this illusory body transcend impermanence?
Man prides himself on his cleverness and guile; Heaven acts with ease, holding firm the reins of command. Though one may suffer some loss, it will ultimately lead to good;
what harm is there in yielding a few steps? When spring arrives, the willows turn green; when autumn comes, the chrysanthemums turn yellow. Splendor and glory are but dreams of the third watch;
wealth and nobility are like the frost of the ninth month. Birth, old age, sickness, and death...
Who can take its place? Sour, sweet, bitter, and pungent—one must bear them all oneself. A single dose of "Nourishing Spirit and Balancing the Stomach" powder;
two servings of "Harmonizing Qi and Draining the Liver" decoction. Before birth, one vainly expends millions of thoughts; after death, there remains but a pair of empty hands.
