Sorrow, joy, parting, and meeting clamor every morning; wealth, honor, poverty, and success keep one busy every day. I urge you: do not strive for superiority. One hundred...
A lifetime spent mingling with the world and the theater; in an instant, the sound of gongs and drums falls silent. One knows not where one’s hometown lies.
For King Udayana, the painted figures have no names;
year after year, suffering and joy are truly boundless. When the years end, life also ends; in the end, one must surely go to the Nine Springs.
Month after month, the ways of the world wax full and then wane; when will this cycle of fullness and deficiency ever cease? In the end, there is nothing to be said.
Day after day, my heart remains ever restless and weary. Alas! The road ahead is difficult; the toils of worldly existence manifest as a house on fire.
From moment to moment, how could the lotus-drip water-clock ever run slow? Yet, unable to taste the nectar of immortality, one vainly errs in one’s practice.
Moment after moment, the light of life passes like a traveler; as every inch of time flows away like a stream, how can one hope to make it stay?
One breath, and then another; at the threshold between humans and ghosts, it is urgent. A single heart of radiant light—cause and effect are surely manifest.
(The Nianfo Verse of Chan Master Yijichewu)
The self-nature is Amitābha; Amitābha is the self-nature. To cling to nature while abandoning cultivation is to turn medicine into disease.
Pure Land is but the mind; the mind is but Pure Land. To discuss the mind apart from the land is a grave error.
Speaking thus of the Lotus Land, tears fall in profusion; the miserable realms of Jambudvīpa are truly pitiable.
Having contemplated thoroughly both the mundane and the supramundane, if one does not call upon Amitābha, whom else could one call?
Deluded for a single thought-moment, one enters the Sahā world; how can one help it that one sinks into it for long kalpas?
If you wish to overturn this defiled land and make it a pure realm, turn the entire mechanism of your being and call upon Amitābha.

I pity myself for having become a monk in this age of Great Peace; though I have understood death and liberation from birth, I have never yet attained it. I only wish that my name be inscribed within the calyx of a lotus flower;
there is no need to be ranked high among those who transmit the lamp.
Urgently and resolutely hold to the Name as if saving one's head from fire; in this Sahā world, there can be no further delay. This very moment, let go of all and return home;
thus, I have already surpassed the former sages by one move.
A single phrase of the Great Name is a precious lotus; with every sound it flows forth from the mind’s own field.
If one can simply maintain this continuity thought after thought, there is no fear that Amitābha will not appear before one.
Knowing that An-yang (Sukhāvatī) is my home, I shall return there and cease from wandering on mistaken paths. Without dwelling on worldly attachments, I shall only recite the Buddha’s name;
thus I shall occupy a precious lotus flower high upon the wondrous pond.

I recall that Amitābha has a prescribed course: ten thousand recitations clearly performed morning and evening. If one simply ensures this is done throughout one's entire life, who would debate whether pure karma is accomplished or not?
Long have the autumns passed since we parted from our homeland; my longing heart for home does not pause for a moment. As Amitābha Buddha thinks of me, I think of him;
we, father and son by nature, are thus united.
A single recitation of Amitābha’s name brings one to stillness; it is as if one has died but not yet been buried.
The debts of many lifetimes in Saṃsāra are now settled; return now to the Pure Land.
The six characters of the Great Name are the Water-Cleansing Pearl; within the square inch of the mind, it is limpid and free from a hundred anxieties. The scenery therein is difficult to describe;
it is like the solitary orb of the moon across ten thousand miles of vast sky.
The Dharma-realm school of the single phrase Amitābha: A thousand gates and ten thousand doors are all encompassed within it. It requires only that pure mindfulness continue without interruption;
Then the reflections of the four lands and three bodies will appear in abundance.
In praise of the blood-painted image of Amitābha Buddha:

Having dried my own finger-blood, I painted this image of Amitābha. What is the intent behind painting this Amitābha? I shall worship it in the evening and pay homage to it in the morning, making constant offerings.
May it guide me at the moment of death out of this Sahā world.
Ashamed and humiliated, I fled to foreign lands; wandering alone, I tasted every bitterness. Recalling this, my bowels break inch by inch;

looking back, tears fall one after another. My fragile fingers are torn as if by knives; blood stains the immeasurable light. How can I repay such compassionate grace? Only this precious incense in a single burner.

Great compassion has perfumed vast eons; from a drop of blood, his entire body appears. This is fundamentally the nature of our innate affinity; when has it ever been separated by so much as a speck of dust?

Out of pity for the suffering of the three realms, he plants the causes for the nine lotuses. Yet, we have not yet returned to our native land; gazing upon him with longing, our tears fall incessantly.

The single phrase of the Buddha-remembrance gāthā, "Amitābha," is the essential heart of our Buddha’s teaching. It penetrates vertically through the five periods and encompasses horizontally the eight teachings.
As for the meaning of this single phrase "Amitābha," those who truly know it are always few, while those who merely listen are far more numerous.
A single phrase of Amitābha opens the gate of rebirth; it is a source of great merit, not a minor root of goodness.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the standard for attaining Buddhahood; by means of the mind that recites the Buddha’s name, one enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
With one phrase of Amitābha, one realizes the three stages of non-retrogression; in this single lifetime alone, one attains the rank of a Buddha.
With one phrase of Amitābha, the gate of Prajñā is opened; the ten directions and myriad dharmas are swallowed whole in a single gulp.
One phrase of Amitābha—vow to perfect it bit by bit; casting aside this single lifetime, become a carefree man.
One phrase of Amitābha—not hurried, not slow; heart and mouth as one, turning it with vivid clarity.
A single phrase of Amitābha—the more one recites, the better it is. It is like a person learning archery: through long practice, one becomes skillful.
Holding the single phrase of Amitābha while closely concentrating the mind is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves.
A single phrase of Amitābha is like drilling for fire: when the wood grows warm and smoke arises, one must not pause.
A single phrase of Amitābha makes the perilous path level as a grindstone, leading straight to the precious abode without lingering at the conjured city.
A single phrase of Amitābha: recite it directly through to the end; take one step to the very bottom. Like a fragrant elephant crossing a river.
A single phrase of Amitābha: it extinguishes fixed karma; like the brilliant sun against light frost, or a flake of snow upon a great furnace.
A single phrase of Amitābha completely transforms the three obstacles; that is, afflictions, karma, and suffering are realized as the secret treasury.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the unsurpassed dhyāna; in one lifetime the task is accomplished, and over vast eons the merit is perfected.
A single phrase of Amitābha is a kōan already fully realized; simply cultivate the heart of resolve, and you will certainly not be deceived.
A single phrase of Amitābha is especially wondrous for awakening the faculty of discernment; when recitation reaches its limit and emotions are forgotten, the cold ashes burst forth like beans.
One phrase of Amitābha; one single master. If these were two separate things, one would need to employ skillful integration.
One phrase of Amitābha leads to the lotus flowers of the nine grades: sow beans and you reap beans; sow melons and you reap melons.
A single phrase of Amitābha requires no laborious synthesis; mind, Buddha, and sentient beings have been one string from the beginning.
This single phrase of Amitābha is the ultimate path; when those of inferior capacity hear it, they laugh out loud in derision.
A single phrase of Amitābha is by no means a trivial matter; it rescues Danxia and calls back Zhaojue.
A single phrase of Amitābha transcends views and surpasses emotions; the seal is broken and the pattern is formed, the water is clear and the reflection appears.
I shall give a brief teaching to the disciple Bodhisattva Jue Ming:
Speak but a single word less; recite a single Buddha-name more. Strike the thought-mind into death, and I will grant that your Dharma-body lives.
With the single phrase "Amitābha," one aspires for birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Only when long practice has reached fruition will one avoid error.
Regarding the liberation and peaceful settlement of Layman Zhou Anshi:
there is no distinct method for cultivation other than taking transcendence as the ultimate goal. While there are many paths to transcendence, the Pure Land is the most direct shortcut.

The time for extinguishing transgressions passes as swiftly as an arrow; days and months flow like a stream. Once the retribution of karma arrives, there is no way to avoid it. Seizing this moment of health and vigor, turn your head with courage and resolve;
let the six sense faculties remain unmoved, and the eight sufferings shall all come to rest.

The Master of the Mind-Only Collection of Vehicles and Precepts, in his leisure from meditation, recites the name of Amitābha with nothing else to do. To deliver sentient beings from the river of craving, he causes all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
Why need one linger with attachment to this Saha world?

I only pray that at the end of life my spirit shall not be disturbed; that I may know in advance when the time has come and remain serene in body; that my skin and flesh shall fall away as the sense-faculties and their objects are purified;
and that I shall entrust my substance to a lotus of the highest grade upon the Golden Terrace.
The pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas becomes intimate through contemplation and recollection;
fundamentally of one essence without distinction, it requires only that the person recognize it as true.
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west; contemplate and behold the Infinite Light in the west. The great earth, mountains, and rivers are not external objects;
the precious awakening of the emptiness of phenomena is the sovereign of the mind.
In this world, it is difficult to obtain this human body; having obtained it, one must take it seriously. How can one repay the boundless and profound kindness of one's parents?
There is no way better than reciting the Buddha’s name to deliver both parents.

Whether in leisure or busyness, motion or stillness, cultivation is not hindered; whether as a farmer, scholar, fisherman, or woodcutter, one may likewise seek it. Whether noble or base, wise or foolish, there is no discrimination;
as long as one recites the six characters, one will find harmony.
Reciting the Buddha's name while living at home, one should practice without ceasing day and night, from dawn until morning;
how much more so when living at home, where there is much comfort, being free from constraints and with a mind empty of conceptual thought.
Whether man or woman, all are capable of cultivation; nothing is more intimate than seeking for oneself. With one voice and one mind, they chant "Buddha";
everyone is sent forth to the bow of the ferryboat.

By whom can the three calamities and eight difficulties constrain? Simply by recollecting Amitābha, they shall not exist where one dwells. Delusion constitutes a sentient being; awakening constitutes a Buddha.
It is solely due to the distinction between delusion and awakening that there is difference.
The sun sets behind the western mountains; I remember my hometown. One must surely examine oneself and prepare the provisions. Readily pack one’s belongings well;
do not wait until the last moment when hands and feet are in a flurry.
Human life is full of affairs and many vexations; even a long life of a hundred years may be difficult to preserve. Amidst the bustle, steal a moment for leisure and recite once:
"Namo Amitābha Buddha"—how excellent!

The burning house offers no peace and endures but briefly; the transformed city can never be one's true ancestral home. If you wish to know the Land of Common Dwelling for both ordinary beings and sages, you must realize that it ultimately returns to the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
Within the realm of True Suchness, there is neither arising nor ceasing; within the Dharma of equality, there is neither self nor other. Whether layperson or monastic, all possess this share:
when spring arrives, where would flowers not bloom?
Flowers of four colors—red, white, blue, and yellow—bloom in full within the pond, as large as chariots. How could ordinary people with mundane eyes ever see them?
Only those who arrive shall know that the fruit does not fail to correspond.

To fully realize the self-nature of Amitābha—what need is there for so much effort? Cease all speculative reasoning regarding the enlightened understanding of the sages and the deluded sentiments of ordinary beings;
with one stroke, cut through the thicket of entanglements.
When the six sense faculties are purified, all Buddhas appear; with a single-minded focus on the sutras they protect and keep in mind, one should praise, extol, and believe in them.
Where else could one find a true companion in the Dharma?

Studying the Way is like ascending a mountain of ten thousand blades; atop the solitary peak, all climbing and grasping cease. One must proceed directly to the place where there is no longer a path to tread before one realizes that heaven and earth are not of this human realm.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. He delivers those with whom he has a karmic affinity. Upon reaching the lotus pond, the flowers bloom without waiting for spring.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. The Buddha-way is inconceivable; suddenly one’s own mind opens, and one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Homage to Amitābha. The Buddha possesses great majestic virtue; he delivers sentient beings of the nine grades, so that they enjoy inexhaustible bliss.
Homage to Amitābha. For the sake of the one great matter, all who are born within my land shall have their heads stroked by me and receive the personal bestowal of prophecy.
Recite the Buddha’s name and do not practice Chan meditation; simply ensure that your resolve is firm. With a single-minded focus that never falters, you will suddenly transcend the three realms.
—From *Influence and Echoes:
A Collection of Pure Land Poems*, by the Bhikṣuṇī Lianghai.
Able to manifest from the Realm of Endurance in the Western Quarter, whenever a person’s faith and aspiration are strong, the World-Honored One of Compassion will always welcome and guide them there;
immediately, he produces the wondrous fragrance of the lotus.
A single phrase of Amitābha accords with the true nature; the nine grades of lotuses encompass the three vehicles.
With a single thought of non-arising, one transcends provisional teachings and may ascend the golden terrace as a successor to Buddhahood.
A single phrase of Amitābha preserves wondrous enlightenment; in the emptiness of nature, both sin and merit leave no trace. Lotus flowers manifest according to the mind;
in listening to the Dharma, always rely upon the World-Honored One.

The principle of Amitābha is fully realized in a single phrase; there is no cultivation, no realization, and no birth. The Dharma King naturally possesses a realm of radiant light, walking step by step upon the ground of lapis lazuli.

The single phrase of Amitābha’s name is the truth of faith and aspiration; the lands of the East and West are not separate from this very person. Within this, the three thousandfold world-system is perfectly encompassed;
tree after tree, flower after flower, all bloom in the same spring.
Recite the single phrase "Amitābha" with certainty; what else can one seek that is superior?

With every sound, it pervades the realm of empty space, stripping away all entanglements like vines from a tree. (The Emperor Sejong of our dynasty said: "Take these four characters, 'A-mi-t'o-fo,' as the very pivot of your practice;
contemplate them for ten thousand years and you will naturally find your own nostrils.")
The essence and function of the single phrase "Amitābha" are true; facing the sun, the entire body is revealed. In a realm beyond yin and yang, one performs somersaults;
in every land and every speck of dust, the Dharma wheel is turned.
A single phrase of Amitābha is recited from the mouth; yet the moment a single thought arises, a thousand layers of separation intervene. How could one’s original truth await the light of reflection?
The infinite sounds of the Buddha are themselves the Dharma-lamp.
A single phrase of Amitābha accords with one’s own mind; the mark of the broad and long tongue is its true knower.
That the Buddhas of the six directions all praise Amitābha together is no ordinary matter of recitation and chanting.
A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha purifies the pulse; revealing the provisional to manifest the real, one awakens to non-arising.
Wherever one goes, the path is perfectly bright and eternally peaceful—what need is there to welcome the three carts outside the gate?

The single phrase of Amitābha is wondrously and uniquely supreme; there is no need to debate the interplay between nature and cultivation. Simultaneously obstructing and illuminating, body and mind are thoroughly penetrated;
the mutual integration of the primary and secondary realms is the gate of non-duality.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the definitive cause; it is the direct path to the Land of Bliss, where the ford is never lost. Why seek further methods for settling the mind?
From the very beginning, the true nature is suchness—the child turning toward its own parent.
Listen truly to the single phrase of Amitābha; with every sound, awaken the person of original nature. A hundred and eight bright pearls revolve in succession;
countless auspicious lights issue from beneath the tongue.
A single phrase of Amitābha’s wondrous turning of the wheel— All Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges praise such a person. In resonance with their voices, the golden platform appears;
Instantly realizing non-arising, one is the Dharmakāya itself.
A single phrase of Amitābha washes away the worldly dust from one’s breast; few know the way beyond the Dharma-body.
The majestic, true Buddha of daily life—refusing to turn back, where else shall one seek?
The single phrase of Amitābha is a most wondrous gate; relying upon these four characters, one emerges from the world.
This Dharma King’s supreme gāthā-medicine can only be taken by swallowing it all at once with a single mouthful.
A single phrase of Amitābha purifies all deluded thoughts; with the adamantine power of firm resolve, one sustains the body. Upon being born in that land, one attains infinite life;
when the flowers bloom beneath the Bodhi tree, there is a spring unlike any other.
A single phrase of Amitābha: all dharmas are level; The six faculties are unimpeded, and the six sense-objects are pure. Originally, the four lands have no high or low;
The fertile field of merit and wisdom requires no tilling.
With the sincerity of a single phrase of Amitābha’s vow-power, one perfectly accomplishes ten recitations and departs for the West.
Even those of the lowest grade surely reach the shore, entrusting their substance to the lotus womb and liberating themselves from the four births.

Recite the single phrase of Amitābha with all one's might; One will transcend the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties. Holding his name extinguishes transgressions and the golden lotus appears;
His compassionate vows rely entirely upon the increase of the Buddha’s power.

A single phrase of Amitābha’s name brings the moon of wisdom to descend; with the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, one's roots of goodness become deep. One directly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression and hastens toward An-yang (Sukhāvatī);
defilements, habitual tendencies, and worldly toil can no longer invade.
A single phrase of Amitābha reveals one’s true nature; turning the light back upon oneself, one escapes from the depths of samsara.
May the waters of the Eight Virtues Pond wash away all the dust of this Sahā world.
Guests passing through from ancient times to the present, they rush about, busy day and night. For what reason do they covet glory? To seek profit, they engage in commerce.
Wealth and nobility bring but temporary pleasure; the hells endure for ten thousand kalpas. The journey ahead is long and far—why not return home early?
Human life does not exceed a hundred years; those who die young are even more pitiable. Moreover, encountering the perils of the world’s path, one travels back and forth, ever shifting and changing.
Affectionate bonds must inevitably end; the karmic ties between enemies and kin remain unresolved. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, free from birth, liberation is naturally secure.
Yet the ocean of karma has never dried, and sentient beings cling everywhere. Turn your head and look back within yourself; all that revolves is but a temporary sojourn.
Simply realize that the fundamental nature is empty; all conditions will naturally fall away. A person who wanders freely without affairs finds peace and happiness wherever they are.
*Pure Land Verse by Chan Master Puren*:
Our Buddha, the King of Great Vows and Compassion, Exhorts people to recite the Buddha’s name and go to the West. Within this Sahā world, one revolves in saṃsāra.

Suffering! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the lifespan is long. If one holds the name for seven days with an undistracted mind, the six sense faculties will become pure and one’s true nature will shine forth clearly.
The Tathāgata points directly to the path of Bodhi; every word and phrase is a clear exposition found within the sacred scriptures.
Every phrase seeks out delusion within emptiness; in that emptiness of delusion, one beholds the true master. At the first sound, it enters stillness; with every sound, there is stillness.
When one dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are penetrated. Do not say that the faculties and sense objects are easy to uproot; you must know that delusive thoughts are most difficult to attack.
Relying solely on the three powers of faith, vow, and practice, sweep away all mundane sentiments, and the nature will naturally harmonize.
The cycles of kalpas are most tragic; for liberation from suffering, none compares to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Focus your mind single-mindedly on Amitābha to leave this world;

diligently uphold the Buddha’s name to enter the Lotus Realm. Amidst the shadows of red banners lie the karmic deeds of past lives; within the thicket of white blades lies the calamity of future rebirths.
Vow that in this life you shall return to the Pure Land, forever departing from the fires of war to go to the West.
The mindfulness of the sound penetrates directly back to before birth; there is no need for the heavy emotions of a boat descending into the water.

With the single phrase "Amitābha" constantly uninterrupted, the six sense-faculties are liberated and one naturally forgets the passing years. Caoxi spoke only of the mind having no dwelling; Sengzhao discussed only the non-transmigration of things.
If you can grasp the subtle and wondrous meaning within these, you will immediately ascend to the lotus flower in the Jade Pond of the Nine Grades.

The arising and ceasing of worldly afflictions are yakṣas; why then do you not sprout the seed of Bodhicitta? Let the field of the mind not grow the weeds of ignorance, for the ground of the nature is always blooming with the flowers of wisdom.
A single phrase of Amitābha is as clear as a mirror, yet the six gates, failing to maintain their guard, fall into chaos like tangled hemp.
I urge you to turn your head and look back early enough; the bitter sea surges on, its shores endless.
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land runs contrary to worldly ways. Do not compare its pure moonlight to former errors. Diligently uphold the Buddha-name as the path of true permanence;

sincerely recite Amitābha’s name and let delusions naturally thin away. Once the six sense-faculties achieve liberation, one will clearly perceive that the four marks of existence are severed from all grasping and reliance.
When merit is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled within the principle of suchness, this is precisely "passing the examination with an empty mind and returning home."
Sitting alone, my mind becomes clear and naturally expansive; letting go of all external conditions, I find joy in this secluded dwelling. The bright moon by the window is my lotus friend;
the pure breeze outside the gate is my companion. A single phrase of Amitābha is ever tranquil; the invocation of the Buddha’s name throughout the six periods remains as it is.
If you wish to know the true message of nianfo, maintain the name within stillness and let it illuminate the great void.
The fisherman profits from his solitary boat; morning and evening he never ceases to cast his hook.
A fine mist shrouds the willow banks; a cold wind drifts over the reed islets. Though gaining profit before one’s eyes may seem good, I fear that Yama will not let you rest.
Facing the Three Heavens with your back turned is ultimately a failure; it is better to recite the Buddha’s name and turn back now.
The woodcutter’s mindfulness of the Buddha grows ever firmer; with every phrase of Amitābha, years pass unnoticed. After the cold rains, fragrant grasses and fallen blossoms lie scattered;
amidst drifting clouds and wild cranes, the setting sun hangs low. Before the cliff, the Western Realm is lush and verdant; beyond the mountains, the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is green and serene.
If one recognizes this as the true Pure Land within, Amitābha will welcome them in to enter the lotus pond.

This body is but a stinking leather bag; why do you cling to it and fail to contemplate your native land? In this life you have committed boundless transgressions, and in future lives there will surely be retribution.
If you are willing to turn your heart and cultivate the Pure Land, you shall clearly realize the Dharma-nature and board the Compassionate Vessel.
Once the karmic consciousness within your breast is entirely eliminated, you will personally behold Amitābha, the King of Great Vows.
The Ten Empty Melodies of the Pure Sound of the West;

the One State of the Western Hall, the Three Dukes of the Nation. Carriages and horses within the halls of Chang’an; the ranks of dukes and nobles divide their duties, while golden seals circulate in succession.

In playfulness, white-haired, one still yearns for the tolling of the bell. Green mountains, trees forming arched canopies; the ornate pillar and the funerary banner—these bring an end to the dream of the yellow millet.
Behold: all worldly fame and achievement are but emptiness. (Only by emptying all that exists can one momentarily rest from the thick, habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time.)

Ten thousand strings of cash and a thousand measures of grain; the green *qinfu* insects rot in their boxes, and the red mercury decays in the granaries. One compounds medicines and smelts cinnabar, or digs into the earth to bury silver jars.
Gold pits and copper mounds turn into earthen tombs; though there be a "God of Money," he cannot purchase the dream of Nanke.
Behold how the wealth and resources of rival nations are all but empty.
In the Northern Garden and Southern Palace, ten thousand households and a thousand gates pretend to be the Ninefold Imperial City. In the Golden House and the Apang Palace, they dally;

in the Jingu Valley and the Tiantai Caves, the terraces and pavilions are sealed by earth-moss. The mounds and graves of the Half-Sheep Hill, the Qige Pavilion, and the Milou Tower—these too are equal to the dream of Huaxu.
Look at those noble mansions and their fields and gardens—all are now empty.
Green and red flowers bloom; twelve golden hairpins attend young pages. Silk curtains surround cloud-like tresses. In the heart of the flowered silken canopy, passions stir.
Powdered faces and rouge are but cleverly crafted skeletons. Fox-spirits flaunt their charms. When rain disperses and clouds dissolve, one thinks back to the broken dreams of Mount Wu.
Behold how these peerless beauties are all but empty.
The strings vibrate with a tinkling sound; the crimson candles burn low as the music reaches its end. Drums roll for the "Jiangnan Nong" melody; flutes play the "Phoenix of the Qin Tower.
In a fleeting glance, the wind whistles through the white poplars. As funeral songs escort them away, the youths of the Imperial Garden enter together into the dream of the Heavenly Court.
Behold: the sounds of the great earth are all empty.
Fish from the caves and camel humps—ten thousand coins for a single meal are not enough to provide them. Fine wine is served in golden goblets; fatty meats are presented on high platters.
The air of slaughter fills one’s throat. I invite you, sir, to enter the jar. Hunting the deer for the pot, it all turns into a *bānyǎo* dream.
Look at the causes and conditions of food and drink; they are all empty.
The green mother and the yellow father, the customs of marrying off daughters and sons. They entwined their necks beneath red quilts, followed by black-clad children circling their knees.
Now, parting ways, each goes to the west and east. The master and his brother scatter the mandarin ducks; they shatter the dreams of the bears and cubs.
Behold how this circle of kinsmen is entirely empty.

With embroidered tigers and carved dragons, his brilliant brush composes ten thousand scrolls of artistry. He presents his fu at Changyang Palace; the multitude at Yuanying Pavilion seek him out for instruction.
Where, then, does one weep for the autumn wind? The desolate tomb of literature—this entire *Nanhua Jing* is nothing more than Zhuang Zhou’s dream.
Behold how embroidered patterns and literary compositions are all but empty.
A mere youth, yet a hero. Clashing and contending for the space between the horns of a snail. A single meal weighs as a mountain; the pain of a glint of an eye brings the sword.
The world’s path is like a headwind against a ship. What need is there to move mountains? Floating tiles and empty boats do not obstruct the dream of the pines in the wind.
Behold: you and I, kindness and enmity—all are but emptiness.
In this bustling turmoil, let there be no concern for the morning cock or the evening bell. There is no need for the merit of chanting; why labor over praising public cases?
Seek the true Master early. When the wind and banner do not stir, let go of the mental contrivances and shatter the dream upon the round meditation cushion.
Behold how all phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty.

[This concludes] ten poems on the theme of Zheng Cheng De Fu assisting the Sovereign’s person. The rank of the First Dignitary is lofty within the palace halls; Talent and virtue attend the imperial gate; The myriad nations and their borders [are at peace].

Controlling both merit and wisdom, he is most honorable and illustrious. Having deeply planted the seeds of past causes, his external protection is diligent; thus the Buddha-dharma is fortified as a vital bulwark.

Behold: are worldly fame and achievement empty or not? (Precisely because they do not stagnate in emptiness, he is able to manifest bodies everywhere to extensively deliver sentient beings, leading them all together into the Pure Land of Amitābha.)

Jade is emerald green and pearls are crimson; seven-foot coral radiates like a rainbow. The taxes exceed the stipends of high officials, and treasures from the imperial court are offered as tribute—its cultivation is truly inexhaustible.
To glorify the Dharma-offering, gold is spread upon the ground to purchase the Jetavana Grove.
Behold whether the resources of the rival state are empty or not.

Upon the roads and to the east of the city, the ornate pavilions and crimson railings appear identical from afar. Intricate carvings adorn the shimmering silver rafters; flowers and bamboo stretch toward the cloud-capped grottoes.
The season for repaying kindness is at its height. A thousand monks are invited; the blessed ground is boundless. The precious Dharma is reverently upheld.
Look at the noble mansions and fields—empty or not?
Like startled geese and flying swans. Ten *hu* of pearls, yet their value is not yet high. Pure as the phoenix of the immortals;
illusory as the dream of Mount Wu. We vow to be reborn together. With the attendants of Dīpaṃkara, manifesting bodies within the inner chambers, our resolve to deliver the world is profound.

Behold how the peerless beauty of these red faces—Vimalakīrti’s consort Vaidehī and her five hundred handmaidens—was rendered empty on that very day they resolved their minds to be born in the Pure Land of Amitābha.

The sound of the drum and the resonance of the bells are clear and crisp; their flowing tones carry on the distant wind. Common ears are startled by these new performances, yet they imitate the ancient melodies of spring recitations.
Celestial music has long sounded its bells as the West welcomes and sends forth; to pay homage to the Golden Immortal, the *sheng* flutes are blown to their conclusion.
Look at the great earth: are sounds empty or not? Water-cress and green mustard grow;
in the river lands, lotuses and rice are red again. With the spirit of abstinence from wine, one’s vigor soars; with the compassion of abstaining from meat, one’s kindness deepens.
Equal in giving, offerings are arrayed across the three altars. Like the *Gandha-kuṭī* and Vimalakīrti, the bowl-food has boundless use.
Look at the causes and conditions of food and drink—whether they are empty or not.

Amidst the colorful screens and the harmonious tones of lutes and zithers throughout a hundred years, the children grow up reciting poetry and books, while the young grandchildren are doted upon with sweetmeats.
I have heard it said that the elder of the Lü family held high office during the Northern Song; he constantly upheld the heart-lamp of the Triple Gem from generation to generation.
Look at this family circle, gathered together—empty or not empty? (The Lü Gongzhu family has served the Buddha for generations. An ancestor once made a vow before the Buddha, saying:
"May those who do not believe in the Triple Gem never be born into my family.")

Majestic and brilliant; when he takes up his pen, a thousand words flow forth, rich in both diction and meaning. His pathos and elegance surpass those of Pan Yue and Song Yu, while his purity and detachment harmonize with the cries of the phoenix.
He sketches the countenances of the Land of Bliss; through his poems, songs, treatises, and hymns, he reveals the pearl of the heart and awakens one from the dream of saṃsāra.
Look at these brocade-like literary compositions—empty or not?
They form bonds and then attack one another; like shifting rain and turning clouds in an instant. A cup of wine is just offered, and suddenly the white blade strikes with shock and pain.
Grinding and refining further melt it down; yet the true gold remains unmoved. Poisonous drugs and *amṛta* (clarified butter) are but one flavor, serving a thousand purposes.
Look at you and me: are enmity and kindness empty or not?

The evening drum and morning bell are, in one stroke, the same in the monastic rules of the famous mountains. Study and investigate while dwelling in rocky caves; refine yourself through diligent meditation and recitation.
The Buddha-sun is now at its zenith; what use is the glow of fireflies? Shatter the lapis lazuli, startling the multitudes of humans and devas.

(To practice with weariness and decay, seeking the minor fruits of humans and devas, is not as good as resolving to become a Buddha to extensively deliver sentient beings of both pure and defiled realms. Behold the wondrous Dharma: truly eternal, empty yet not empty.
I urge you to read this poem, profound and subtle, beyond words, transcending beginning and end. The Dharmakāya is fundamentally neither West nor East;

yet out of compassion for the tormented realm of Sahā, it specifically manifests the glory of the adornments of Sukhāvatī. You must believe that the lotus blooms through a single thought-moment; do not allow the weeds to choke it by failing to protect it.
A thousand clusters arise; ten thousand transgressions revolve—You should weary of them. Try to manifest once the pure and wondrous light of the mind.

Exhort yourself to make this vow with a resolute heart, vowing to reach the Land of Bliss. The true realm of that Land of Bliss is peerless, far surpassing the six heavens of desire and all the dhyānas.

Beautiful and pure, she utterly transcends the confusion of celestial Māras and non-Buddhist paths. Her lifespan is immeasurable; one need not inquire after her years. Her female faculties are fully transformed as the poison first descends.
She advances in cultivation and makes offerings, constantly hearing the Dharma. Adorned with elegant ornaments, she upholds the Buddha’s banner.
I exhort you to guard right mindfulness;
the precious nature of the lotus has resplendent branches upon branches. Four colors intermingle in a wondrous form:
emerald leaves float in circles around elegant buds, and fine gold is wrought to reflect in the deep pool. A womb such as this is truly worthy of entrustment; its substance is flawless and sublime.
One should reflect upon this. When the merit of ten recitations is perfected, one dwells among the superior ranks. I ask you: is it better to come early or late?

I urge those with deep attachments to lead their kin and followers out of the mundane dust. The halls and pavilions soar above the void as they open their faces toward the West, where one should go to pay homage.
Exquisite! To rest from the eastern lands and speak of a worthy matchmaker—once the dream has awakened, how could there be both fragrance and jade?

Having cultivated to the point of eliminating both joy and sorrow, one attains pure abiding through a single instance of childlike innocence. The root of craving is washed away, leaving no room for lingering hesitation.

I exhort you: human affairs and worldly occupations leave the consciousness in a vast blur; what is their fundamental source? Worldly sentiments are as fickle as shifting weather—cold one moment, warm the next.

One may find joy and delight in speech at this very instant, yet in a mere blink of an eye, one sighs in darkness, suddenly encountering grievance. Such topsy-turvy confusion is truly endless; who has the skillful means to provide aid?
Return to the source; enter deeply through one gate to cultivate the Western Path. Shake off the spirit and decline worldly clamor.

I urge you, young men and women, who are born ignorant and most pitiable: do not let the six consciousnesses dwell perpetually amidst clouds and mist. Each of you possesses the Bodhi-mind from many lifetimes past.
Planting these four characters truly creates a field of merit and wisdom. A long life or an early death merely teaches the deluded to follow their shadows and echoes;
success or failure is but a vain recognition of one's own folly or worth. Amidst the clamor of myriad dharmas, who can achieve purity? None compare to planting jade lotuses in the Western Pond.

Exhorting toward impartiality, crossing over with purity, cultivating purity, awakening to purity, and containing pure light—impartiality from its origin is free from duality or three. When the fish attains the celestial body, it can receive the prediction;

when the dragon encounters the golden-winged bird, what more could it endure? (When attachments dissolve and emotions are exhausted, who is small and who is great? The Śrāvakas make vows to deliver the swarms of bees. (Maudgalyāyana)
The Great Being divided his body to investigate the class of frogs; (Mañjuśrī) taught the six-syllable mantra to be recited by a parrot. The blue lotus entrusts its tongue to hold it;
listen to the sound of the Buddha’s name.
The sound of reciting the Buddha’s name merges with the Dharma-realm; every sound revolves throughout the great void. Where the mind’s sound penetrates, the light of the mind shines brilliantly;
the sounds and lights of all myriad things are within a single mirror.
In the Pure Land, one utterly casts aside the riches and nobility of the immortals; incense, flowers, pearls, and water settle in profound stillness. Celestial music is heard from no known source;
the wind blows through the jeweled trees, producing melodic sounds.
Soaring freely through the expanse of emptiness, a heroic spirit transcending the three realms; a single practice of *samādhi* to convey the essential message,
a four-character true scripture for spiritual cultivation—
this is composed to awaken those lost in delusion.

The human body exists as a reward for merit; I urge you not to be deluded amidst the red dust of the world. Ignorance is entirely like poisoned wine; once awakening occurs, one is like a swan in the mud.

External objects are illusory, a chaotic mix of the beautiful and the ugly; emotions are manifold, blending laughter and weeping. Auspiciousness is but a dream of the deer; song and dance are all but the cicadas in the vinegar.

The flower is most beautiful when it blooms; the branch rests securely where it finds support. Once cast adrift, it inevitably perishes in the north; through skillful means, it is reborn only in the west.

As long as conditions are free from delusion, why worry that encounters may not be equal? When the mind is empty, one truly passes the imperial examination; unmoving, one illuminates the world to its very limits.
May we together dwell in stillness and recite the Buddha’s name;
may we together unroll this scroll and speak of our lives. When the mirror and the lamp interact, their radiance is sufficient;
may we achieve the purity of the highest grade of the Lotus Land.
A single phrase of Amitābha truly opens the gate of skillful means. Moment after moment, without interruption, the myriad dharmas merge into true mindfulness.
With every sound, one continuously recites the name of Amitābha; letting go of the dusty mind, one gains great power. Shadows depart and shadows arrive—where is their limit?
Like a mirror-disk, it must be polished for a long time until the end.

The True Sect is fundamentally beyond words; how can I teach you to speak of something out of thin air? Hearing that even the various heavens have not yet attained realization, it is better to rejoice and recite the name of Amitābha.
Heaven’s will pities the secluded grasses; the human world prizes the late-day clearing. In old age, I cultivate the Pure Land; from now on, my life shall be fulfilled.
Lifting up [the name) that fills all space, the Blissful Land lies therein. Its sounds are limitless, yet through their winding turns they form a resonant clarity.
(A single burst of tears, several bodies of sweat—this is the news of the turning-over of the body for one who truly recites the Buddha’s name.)
Transformations of views and intentions cause confusion, their outward appearances diverging; when ordinary fools reach this point, they are all utterly muddled.
When a single bubble arises, the entire ocean vanishes, leading one body after another to fail as a true man.

Within sameness there is difference; within difference there is sameness. When the provisional and the real, the high and the low, are all illumined at once, clinging attachments are entirely dissolved and the mind’s capacity becomes vast.
The stages of the holy and the ordinary fill all of empty space.
A single thought can truly transform the holy or the mad; that the ignorant do not believe this is truly lamentable. Of what use is reading ten thousand scrolls of books?
It only adds another dream to the cycle of saṃsāra.
How great is the mind of the immeasurable Sage! It swallows and spits out the void, surveying past and present. The Way resides in the radiance; the scriptures reside on paper.
There is no need to say it is shallow, nor to say it is deep.
I urge you to practice correctly;
it is all because of attachment to this suffering Sahā world that you take up saṃsāra and undergo torment. Morning and night you toil in vain, with not a single thing accomplished.
You should know how matters truly stand.
I recite one scroll of the Amitābha Sūtra as my daily practice; my mind has attained the "first place" in emptiness, and my dream has finally awakened.
Turning my head to carefully reckon the affairs of this dusty world, they are all but the forms of ants upon a golden wheel.
Beholding Amitābha is a supreme and distinct encounter; one dose of Qingliang breaks the deep intoxication. Sudhana has already entered the Lotus Pond Assembly;
he no longer remembers his childhood—fifty-three years [of practice] (guided thus by the King of Vows, Samantabhadra).
In the emptiness of nature, where is there a Sahā world? Amidst a mass of fire, lotuses bloom through the power of vows. A single phrase transcends immeasurable dharmas;
when the sense-faculties and their objects dissolve, that is Amitābha.
Making the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name as an act of giving—what further private gain could there be between the human realm and the heavens? Do not say that this mindfulness has no flavor;
when the flowers finally bloom, you shall behold the Buddha.

The Divine hears (exiting the mouth and entering the ears; with the Divine containing it, the numinous light internally perfumes, so that the faculties and objects are about to fall away; thus, I expound this in stillness).
Extraordinary blessings will surely return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Even before departing for the West, one has already attained purity and coolness.
Wondrous sounds emerge from the lotus tongue; a single phrase of Amitābha is fragrant in every character.
How sorrowful that my life lacks freedom; relying on others for plans only drags out my grief. Hearing the Buddha’s name in stillness is like awakening anew;
how could I, from now on, cling to a bubble upon the sea?
Fragrant breezes waft gently through the autumn mist. They are neither ordinary men nor immortals. With a single thought of Amitābha, one transcends form and appearance;
the resonance of his voice vibrates as the moon reaches its full orb.
This voice is like jade, yet even more like gold; it transcribes the single heart of Amitābha. There naturally comes the news of non-arising;
how many connoisseurs are there among humans and gods?

When the vessel and the single sound have already reached boundless merit, how much more so when every sound is prolonged through right mindfulness? Hearing them as they enter like thunder, there is no distinction between self and other;
they cause one to recall the King of Drum-Sounds.
Without warning, the autumn colors come from the west; as the night deepens in stillness, the painted horns sound mournfully. The heart of the heroic man seeking fame and merit does not die;
may he rise upon a golden terrace from the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The sound of the mind manifests universally, and the nature of boundless hearing is opened all at once; it reaches upward to the distant heavens and descends to the nine realms below.
It reflects and resonates with the light of my mindfulness, and countless numinous spirits all return.

The Spirit of the Contemplated Realm (Repeatedly refined through cultivation, discarding the coarse to attain the subtle; the realization of rebirth is not based on empty words, and thus it is further modeled here):
A single utterance of the Buddha’s name awakens the faculty of hearing; one visualizes the World-Honored One in the West. Its transcendent resonance flows forth, surpassing all forms and appearances;
the soaring mind manifests a separate, wondrous universe.

The Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) realm-sea, wherein purity and defilement are fully interpenetrated, manifests completely as the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). As the supreme lotus cultivation extends throughout the measure of the entire Dharma-realm, it is thus revealed:

within the infinitely layered and inexhaustible ten threads, the Dharma-realm of Ultimate Bliss and Flower Adornment is pervasive. When one recites the name of Amitāyus, every sound resonates through all;
within a single lotus palace, there are myriad lotus palaces.
The wind blows through its transcendent melody, circling a thousand flowers; To make offerings to Amitābha is to offer to Śākyamuni. Who among men beyond the heavens can harmonize with this tune?
Floating pavilions in the sky shimmer like clouds and dawn light.

The star-bannered deities come and go to the site of enlightenment; infinite heroic spirits emerge from the river of craving. Sitting upright in the void, they enter meditative concentration together;
throughout the east and west, past and present, all are Amitābha.

As soon as it was said that the West manifests in the ten directions, the ten directions are but the single Dharma-King. The majesty and spiritual power of the Dharma-King’s name shake heaven and earth;
all internal and external māras and illusions vanish like shadows.
The local scenery is originally free from delusion and relies upon the truth; a single radiance of mind pervades every land and dust mote.
Within the square inch of the heart, the numinous clarity contains the Pure Land—who, then, would lack a favorable cause for rebirth there?
The matter of birth and death is of great importance; impermanence is swift. Concentrate your mind and spirit to reach the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Having read but ten years of books throughout my life, how could our meeting be so late? May our vows not differ. Let us plant lotus seeds to fulfill our old promise;
rebirth in this auspicious realm is by no means empty talk.
In this Sahā world, I have long wished to cast off my robe of toil; with a single deep thought, I go forth and return again.
Vowing together to repent and eliminate the faults of body, speech, and mind, may we fly out together through the barrier of birth and death.
With ease, he turns the wondrous wheel of the Dharma King; with infinite excellence, he transcribes the One True Reality.
A noble disciple who has perfected the site of enlightenment, where both Sahā and Sukhāvatī are eternally in spring.
Grains of silt and mud are exchanged for golden sand; if one is willing to leave this Sahā world, one has reached home.
Everywhere they fly, supported by the soles of their feet—who would say that flowers do not grow upon dry land?
In long and short lines, you and I:
under a pale moon and sparse lamps, we skillfully capture this cool, limpid resonance. You and I: with sutras and incense, let us forge a deep and profound faith.
You and I: knowing one another, there is not a single trace of illness. You and I: our hearts through countless kalpas...
The vow: May the single mirror of perfect fusion reflect all; may you transform worldly conditions into pure conditions. How could there be both the Buddha’s seal and the Mara’s seal?
Between you and me, let us make a lotus-pact for every lifetime.
I and you share this natural, celestial bond; it does not depend on mere conformity. I and you have made a lotus-like covenant in our hearts—a precious stream and golden waves.
I and you shall meet again and again, with no other intent. I and you must exhort one another: do not let the moment slip away.
Throughout our lives, we have secretly sought refuge in peace and joy; for a hundred years, as pure youths, we have relied upon the Buddha.
You and I—rejoicing, we depart from Saṃsāra. You and I—like a gentle breeze and sweet nectar, a single point of true principle. You and I—cooling and perfectly suited, seamless.
Celestial robes, I give them to you; the lotus-land seas are rare amidst the mundane dust, I give them to you. One Buddha and his followers dwell together in reliance.

With earnest devotion, our vows are interconnected and secure; the silent, wondrous sounds are exquisite and even more subtle. I give them to you; together we shall return to the West in full perfection.

Throughout my life’s affairs, I have wandered without relying on my own mind; in this silence, those among humans and devas who share my resolve are few. Now the precious flower and the moon of wisdom arrive in their season;
moved by gratitude, I have met one who understands my music.
May all fellow practitioners of the same vow sit together upon lotus pedestals. When I am born in the Pure Land, may each and every lotus flower bloom.
In stillness, there is but one flavor, fundamentally cool and refreshing; I shall not seek other realms within the celestial palaces of immortals.
With the hundred-and-eight *bodhi*-beads held in my hand, I shall inscribe the wondrous fragrance of the lotus upon every thought.
This mind has already blossomed together with the precious flower; the lotus-faith first arrives from the Pure Land. Not departing from the single truth, it follows the pulse of Buddhahood;
may we sit together upon the purple-golden terrace.
The setting sun and bright moon lie west of the small bridge; human figures and the fragrance of lotuses enter the field of vision together.
Hearing that Amitābha’s compassionate vows are fulfilled, I incline my heart to first offer the purple *liuli* (ox-head wine).
I send my sincere regards through paper and ink; whenever I face the Lotus Land, I think of you. Facing the western wind from afar, I frequently send these words:
may we together cultivate the fragrance of the treasury of radiant Dharma.

The precious resonance flows vast and deep, its subtlety penetrating the minute; from the ten directions, the rain of flowers is just now falling. May we never forget the covenant forged in life after life;
may our practice of the single-grade lotus not fail to fulfill its vows.
The first light appears, purple and shimmering; it illuminates my heart’s aspiration to reach the West.
Hearing that Amitābha’s compassionate vow is most earnest, he extends his golden arm from afar to lead me forth.
News from the Lotus Land (With Preface) The true essence of Great Master Miaokong is pure, clear, and luminous; it does not belong to any single side, yet it fully encompasses all phenomena.
Through a single thought at the beginningless past, ignorance suddenly arose, whereby space manifested within this fundamentally pure and original state.
The Great Earth is like a lamp within a mirror and a mirror within a lamp; the six realms and four modes of birth are layered upon one another without end.
All sages and ordinary beings alike emerge from the world, reflecting and manifesting in a continuous cycle, never ceasing their transformative deliverance.
How far-reaching is this! In the life of a human being, for ten months there is blood and qi, and for three years there is milk and turbidity.

From one lifetime to many lifetimes, one takes the reflected shadow as the mind and the four great elements as the body. Birth follows death, and death follows birth; form and spirit circulate in flux.
One cannot mend the leaks at the heart of the river, only emptying increasing the sorrow within a dream. There are a thousand varieties of suffering and joy, and [the cycle of] kindness...
The myriad transformations of enmity are clearly the workings of cause and effect; yet those caught in the midst of it remain utterly deluded—this is truly a matter for deep lamentation.
This book explains these matters layer by layer, stripping away the coarse and mundane while its subtle, profound essence gives rise to all manner of wonders.
It is the single path home that guides me forward; through its nine grades of text, it reveals the extraordinary skillful means of rebirth in the Pure Land.
Thus, sentient beings are benefited and brought together in peace and happiness. The Pure Land manifests in its perfection, and the Sahā world is instantly emptied.
The Buddha-land becomes one’s home; lotus flowers rest upon one’s feet. Like reflections in a mirror of radiant light, there is not the slightest trace of flaw.
Do not undergo further transmigration, lest you give rise to manifold sufferings.
The Two Honored Ones divide the two lands to save the deluded masses through the Dharma; to encourage those dwelling in the East to turn their minds directly toward the West.
Originally manifesting from within the mind, the light encompasses many worlds. From this moment on, proceeding straight ahead, in every thought-moment one shall behold Amitābha.

Those with the karmic affinity receive ordination together; long have they been graced by the Buddha’s manifold kindness. Transforming the multitudes of this Sahā world, his radiance leads them out of the river of craving.
With single-minded earnestness, praise Amitābha and the wondrous adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. May all people, without exception, swiftly depart for the Western Quarter.
The most wondrous and profound mechanism is straightforward and without curvature; it is neither shallow nor deep, for the Buddha-mechanism is inherently complete.

A single radiance shines upon the ten directions; majestic and unmoving, the King of Dharmas. Though the three calamities arise in boundless worlds, the Pure Land stands tall with its banner of the seven treasures.
The light of Amitābha shines boundlessly upon the great earth, the void, and the distant heavens. Where is there a place for people to gather and take refuge?
There are blue, yellow, red, white, and purple-gold lotuses.
There are no more demons, heretics, or weapons; a single expanse of radiant glory reveals the Buddha. All those of supreme goodness gather together;
transformed birds and celestial music abound throughout the six periods of the day.
How marvelous! A single thought evokes the Western Land; through his guidance, one is born into great auspiciousness. This Sahā world is truly a realm of burning affliction;
it is better to return [to the Pure Land] and find immediate coolness.
I have perfected my single mind: reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha. From now on, the surging waves of the oceans of lands in the ten directions shall cease.
When will this mutual strife and killing ever end? We exchange skulls and yet give rise to further enmity; whether intentional or unintentional, all is but karma.
We treat the lives of others as delicacies for our own feasts.
Day and night one is busily occupied with no leisure; when will gold and jade accumulate like mountains? The seats of humans and devas shift in turn;
the treasury and storehouse wealth deities change their watches again.

The suffering in hell is extreme; the mind is clouded and evil remains undispelled. Enduring pain for long years is truly hard to bear. Through a thousand births and ten thousand deaths, one’s physical form changes, yet in an instant, the *āpānaka* demons brandish their knives once more.

Pitiable are the animals, whose births and deaths never cease; their lives are cheap and their bodies light, lacking spiritual awareness. Yet they still strive for dominance, committing mutual acts of lust and slaughter;
the mental affairs of animals are truly fragmented and trivial.

The hungry ghosts are desolate and drifting; the realm of ghosts is filled with sorrow. They toil in bitter hardship, driven by winds and thunder. In their poverty, they further suffer the retribution of having their bodies burned.
Layer upon layer of illusory forms, their pain shall not turn back.

Having fortunately attained this human body in the realm of men, it is not yet secure; in a hundred years, one must pass through the barrier of death in an instant. A single point of borrowed silver cannot follow one beyond;
what can be endured of a lifetime of toil and hardship?

Asuras and humans contend with one another over self and others, facing victory or defeat; flying sand and rolling stones kill people’s hearts. The asuras suffer greatly, intoxicated by their campaigns of war;
in their restless dreams, they dwell in forests of swords and arrows.

Those who cultivate the ten wholesome paths of the heavenly way dream of entering heaven; those who diligently seek secret formulas become immortals among the multitudes. Yet, as long as their karmic fetters are not extinguished, they remain subject to birth and death;
their immeasurable spirits all fall back into the peripheral realms.
Alas! To slander Prajñā is to disturb the true mind at every turn, leading to error throughout a thousand lifetimes; when will a favorable sound be heard?
Turning one's back on awakening, one possesses no knowledge; may the Awakened One come to deliver us, manifesting the power of skillful means to utterly destroy greed, hatred, and delusion.
Taking those very people amidst the dust, transform them into companions beyond the dust. May you turn over the grace of the Tathāgata and aspire to go to the Western Land.
When one awakens, the great dream is ended; when unaware, the dream is still in full swing. Enduring suffering through saṃsāra, on what day shall we return to the mountain of our home?
Striking down layer upon layer of obstacles, one naturally attains a state of total clarity and coolness. Alas, the ocean of dust remains vast and boundless;
within these hindrances, further hindrances arise.
Failing to escape the circle, the deluded dreams and spirits are many; mishearing the words of others, one once again enters the net.

In every place, the banners stand firm as the wind enters meditative concentration; tier upon tier, the pavilions and towers harbor the radiance of jewels. When the human mind reaches this state, it is entirely free from defilement;
all is the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s liberation.
The water of eight virtues reflects golden sands; within ponds of the seven treasures bloom flowers of the nine grades. Birds exhort people to diligently practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
throughout the six periods of the day, celestial music resounds without clamor.

Do not recite the scriptures, nor practice seated meditation; there is no other Buddha-dharma to transmit to you. Simply take this single phrase, "Namu Amida Butsu," and use it as the causal condition for the Western Pure Land.
Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha all possess past affinities. From now on, they shall no longer fall among the realms of humans or devas.
By diligently drawing forth the radiance of the mind, the lotus flowers of the nine grades will surely manifest before them.

How magnificent are the virtues of Amitābha in Sukhāvatī! Upon the precious lotus pedestals of that Cool and Pure Land, transformed birds raise their voices day and night, calling forth the opening of the human heart-mind.
The spirit transcends beyond the three realms; the mind manifests within a single sound. Essence and function are clearly present; boundless power of thought is heroic.
Saha world, Saha world, Saha world—whose sorrows can be counted? Endless ascents and descents follow the wind-wheel;
it is difficult to find a foothold, and one often loses one's place. Appearing and disappearing in Jambudvīpa, one cannot remain still; the head has changed its form to become what it is today.
Ancient one! Why did you not contemplate Amitābha sooner to escape the sufferings of this Sahā world?
The bliss of the West! The bliss of the West! The bliss of the Western Land is entirely without effort; it arises spontaneously through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.
The wind blows through the nets of trees, forming celestial music; pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas enter the One Vehicle. Among humans and devas, there are only good paths and no three evil realms.
Why not contemplate Amitābha early on, so as to receive the bliss of the Western Land?
The Patriarch spoke clearly: "Listen closely, all of you. There is no second path home; one Buddha is eternally efficacious.

If you accomplish the task through diligent effort, never allow yourself to succumb to negligence. With single-mindedness and without regression, the flower will bloom and the precious moon will descend."
One Buddha is concentration; single-minded mindfulness is wisdom. When mindfulness enters the Buddha-wisdom, true samādhi is accomplished.
The resonance of the lotus is naturally pure; its light is perfect and its vital energy sufficient. The Sahā world is chaotic and lacks clarity; it remains submerged in the various desires.
"One Buddha is infinite Buddhas; do not harbor various dualistic views. Those who wholeheartedly keep Amitābha in mind are protected and remembered by every Buddha.
If the mind’s thoughts arise in scattered flight, not a single one can be realized. If you seek power elsewhere, Amitābha will no longer be true."
When the pure mind finally enters the channels, the true essence vanishes in a state of daze. At the place where vows and vows intermingle their radiance, Amitābha delivers this person.
If one wishes to go, one goes immediately; if one wishes to stay, one stays immediately. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the immeasurable light shines forth—a brilliantly clear, single path.
A single phrase of four characters sends you to the Western Land. If you worry that you cannot go, you had better settle the matter early.
This is the ordinary handiwork of a master; it brings forth the spontaneous fragrance of the lotus. Do not say that spiritual practice lacks rules;
by following what has been taught, one becomes cool and refreshed.
A single step into the air is most serene; the lotus appears in the mind and brings auspiciousness. Do not say that there are no nine grades therein;
from the very beginning, a single thought is the Western Land.
The Western Path (with Preface). By Dharma Master Gu Kun.
As for calling the single phrase "Amitābha" the "Path," it is that which cuts across the source of delusion horizontally and casts one directly into the ocean of awakening;
it is the most simple, the most direct, and the great skillful means. Thus the Sūtra says: "If a person merely recites..."
"Amitābha. This is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna. The Essential Explanation states:
"One should know that upholding the Name is both simple and direct, yet it is also sudden and perfect, because every thought-moment is itself the Buddha.
There is no need for visualization, nor is there any necessity for investigation; it is perfectly luminous right now, complete without remainder or deficiency. The Direct Pointing states:

The Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment universally accords with the capacities of sentient beings, delivering the Dharma in over three hundred assemblies, causing all living beings to equally realize the true and eternal.

If one seeks that which accords with their capacity and resonance, where the affinity between the seeker and the Buddha is profound, which is most simple and easy, and whose merit is supreme and its path most direct, none surpasses the single gate of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Moreover, as for the five...
In times when defilements are rampant, the afflictions of sentient beings are heavy; practicing in other paths will surely make accomplishment difficult.
If one does not rely upon this gate, by what means could one swiftly escape birth and death?

For this reason, the Teacher of the Sahā world has exhorted us repeatedly, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have earnestly encouraged us to go, and throughout thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, they everywhere point toward this as the ultimate destination. Go!
The sages of antiquity and the worthies of the present—all have turned toward this. How magnificent!

This single phrase, "Namu Amida Butsu," can truly be called the compassionate vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and the direct path to birth in the Western Land. In the past, the Venerable Shandao devoted himself exclusively to this;
that the multitude hailed him as an emanation of Amitābha—how could they be deceiving us? To examine his own practice and his transformation of others...
In short, nothing exceeds the wondrous purport of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. It states: "Sentient beings have heavy obstructions; their objects are subtle while their minds are coarse;

their consciousnesses flutter and their spirits fly away, making visualization difficult to accomplish. Therefore, out of great compassion, the Great Sage directly exhorts them to single-mindedly recite the Name.
Precisely because reciting the Name is easy, if it is continuous, one will be born [in the Pure Land]. If one can maintain this mindfulness..."
Maintain the continuity of mindfulness until the end of life as your appointed term. Recite ten times and you will be reborn ten times; recite a hundred times and you will be reborn a hundred times.

Chan Master Chewu said: "If one sets aside the Buddha's name to separately cultivate the holy practices of the Three Vehicles, it is a waste of one's spirit and energy—it is like drawing the trigger of a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt to kill a mere field mouse.
How much more so if one creates the karmic conditions for rebirth within the six realms of ordinary existence?"
It is the karma of death.
This single phrase, "Amitābha," was spoken with ultimate compassion. Upon hearing this Dharma so difficult to believe, one should vow to be born in that land.
This single phrase, "Amitābha," possesses inconceivable lifespan; both he and all his people are entirely without distinction.
A single utterance of "Amitābha" possesses the power of immeasurable merit. Like a great stone placed upon a boat, one will certainly not sink.

A single utterance of "Amitābha" eliminates the sins of immeasurable kalpas; if merely hearing the name brings liberation from suffering, how much more so for those who recollect it with earnest devotion!

A single phrase of "Amitābha": in the age of the Dharma’s decay, this affinity is the deepest. Other practices are difficult to accomplish; only this one alone transcends all others. A single phrase of "Amitābha":
it is the diverse skillful means of all Buddhas. Those who wish to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing should recite it with single-minded devotion.
A single phrase of Amitābha is proclaimed by a thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises. That Buddha and we share a great karmic affinity from past lives.
A single phrase of Amitābha—Huiyuan knew its profound mystery; its merit is supreme and progress is most easy. To recite the Buddha’s name is the foremost practice.
A single phrase of Amitābha: the Lotus Pond possesses right view. At the moment of death, he bestowed compassionate instruction: "Simply recite with sincerity. A single phrase of Amitābha:
its spiritual power is unfathomable. Even a parrot chanting the Buddha’s name was reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

(*Wǎngshēng jí* states: There was a man from Tánzhōu who kept a myna bird. The bird would often recite the Buddha’s name. When it died, he buried it in a coffin. Suddenly, a single blue lotus flower sprouted, emerging from its mouth. One who composed a verse about this said:

“There was a spiritual bird named Bāgē, Who understood how to follow the monk’s words and recite Amitābha. Now dead and buried in level ground, a lotus has blossomed; If people do not turn their hearts back [to the Dharma], what can they do?”)*
The Merit of Reciting the Buddha’s Name with a Distracted Mind (with Preface) The *Dharmapada-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra), as expounded by the ancient Dharma Master Kun, states:
"If a person, even with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and recites 'Namo Buddha' but once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
A poem from the Western Chamber reads: "The soul flies and the mind is scattered; the name of the Buddha [destroys] sin."
Melted away. The lotus blossoms like the rising sun, and one ascends to the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss. The *Secret Treasury Guide* states:
"If one has deep faith and earnest aspiration, yet during the practice of nianfo (buddha-recitation) the mind is frequently distracted, this constitutes the lowest grade of birth.
Although the flower opens slowly for those born in the lower grade, their bliss surpasses that of the celestial palaces, and they are forever liberated from saṃsāra, attaining a station of rank."
I shall not regress. Reverently adhering to this intent, I compose these verses:
Holding the Name while distracted is of great merit; The Sūtra clearly records this within the *Lotus*. Reciting even a single phrase leads to Buddhahood;
By reciting much, one knows that virtue and wisdom are fulfilled.
Holding the Name even amidst distraction brings great merit; transcending horizontally while still bearing karma is most perfectly harmonious.
Such are the wondrous differences within Amitābha’s ocean of vows, which all Buddhas praise with inexhaustible admiration.

Holding the Name with a distracted mind is of great merit; one’s rebirth will not fall into the city of doubt. Though there may be temporary distinctions of high and low among the nine grades, in the end, one’s adornments will be equal to those of the Buddha.
Holding the name amidst distraction is of great merit; it fully integrates the boundless ocean of teachings. Simply rely on counting recitations and maintain constant single-minded mindfulness;
there is no need to first seek the emptiness of discursive thoughts.
Holding the Name with even a distracted mind brings great merit; the dark paths receive illumination and all are traversed. Do not let the Buddha-sun set behind the western mountains;
for who would fear even a million layers of clouds of delusion?
Holding the Name amidst distraction is of great merit; Amitābha’s compassionate embrace is boundless.
No matter how various thoughts may constantly intrude and disturb, recite the Buddha’s name with vigor and never let it slacken.
Holding the Name amidst distraction is of great merit; it is like a hero appearing in a time of chaos. One need not fear thousands upon thousands of bandits and thieves;
one only requires that the general’s wisdom and strength be sufficient.
**Verses on Chanting the Buddha’s Name to Open the Mind (with Preface)** By Dharma Master Gukun Since I first began studying the Pure Land school,
whenever I have encountered those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, I have observed that some are attached to the "gate of awakening."

If the mind is not open and unobstructed, or if it gives rise to evil, resentful, or deluded thoughts, and the heart becomes filled with sorrow, then due to these two conditions, one cannot exhaust the thieving mind through death and fail to recite the Buddha’s name with all one's might. Thus, Master Chegewo said:
"Regarding the single gate of the Pure Land, at the very beginning one seeks the gate of awakening; in the end, without waiting for wisdom to arise, wisdom arises of itself. It is not...
One must repent of one's karma, and the offenses will naturally vanish; without severing the afflictions, delusions will naturally become empty.
This is the ultimate in brevity and essentiality, the ultimate in directness and swiftness. When its realization is attained, it is the ultimate in vastness and the ultimate in finality.
One need not seek awakening in the Lotus School; one must simply protect the six great characters of the Name.
If you can hold them in your mouth at every moment, every sound will call out to the True Heavenly Father.
In the Lotus School, there is no need to seek awakening; one should simply fix upon a certain number for Amitābha.
If one can recite it a hundred thousand times every day, at all times one will constantly tread the path back to the source.

Reciting the Buddha’s name attains wondrous single-mindedness; this wondrous recitation is inexhaustible. Without needing to seek through inquiry, the principle naturally penetrates. Reciting until the moment of death, one is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
thus, in an ordinary way, one greatly revives the ancestral tradition.

Single-minded recitation of the Buddha’s name is wondrous and inexhaustible; Temporarily arriving in the Land of Common Residence, the four lands merge as one. Among those still bound by fetters, many are Bodhisattvas on the verge of Buddhahood;
Within the sound of a gentle breeze, the True Doctrine is proclaimed.

Single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name is wondrous and boundless; it is the supreme lineage personally transmitted from the Golden Mouth. All Buddhas bear witness to this with their broad and long tongues;
even the most ignorant man or woman can fully penetrate it.

through the three miserable realms and eight difficult conditions, there is no suffering we have not tasted. Life and death roll on in vast waves—when shall liberation be expected? Now that we have encountered...

The Supreme Vehicle. Having attained the subtle faith, one hears the Dharma of the Pure Land and knows with certainty where to return. Though one may be diligent, there is regret that progress is slow;
yet if one is indolent, rebirth will be impossible. Now, this book is carved for the universal benefit of those of like mind, to admonish body and mind and serve as an aid for the Pure Land.
Establishing a long-term practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) as the way to return to the Western Paradise, I universally pray:
May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm who hear this lotus sound together plant roots of goodness. We humbly pray that our parents, teachers, and monks;
our enemies and kin from kalpas past; and all spirits and insects may receive the light of Amitābha’s vows and the compassionate power of Avalokiteśvara.
May their three obstructions be instantly eliminated and the four lands be perfectly purified. The verse says:
The mind penetrates the flow of Dharma, transforming all obstacles; Faith, vow, and practice perfected, one transcends birth to reach the Lotus Realm.

Universally benefiting the ten directions, the liberation of sentient beings is swift; Through the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance, one circulates throughout the Dharma-realm, wherein the one encompasses all.
Perfectly interfused and without exterior, every dharma is spiritually efficacious; Every mind is sovereign and free.
Emptying this Sahā world, may all beings together be born in Pure Tranquility; always maintaining this mind, never be indolent in the future.
